author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
content:
The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.
Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”
The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.
Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.
“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”
The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
content_c:
Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
October 23, 2026
As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."
The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.
Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name — or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?
"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."
Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.
This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.
But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.
How do names shape first impressions
Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."
Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness.
For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.
"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.
'Weirdness': Why people react negatively to some names
In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.
Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.
Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.
Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.
"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.
Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.
"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."
Pain, now 41, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.
"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"
Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.
How humor helps — and harms — as a coping mechanism
As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.
Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."
"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."
Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.
"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"
How an embarassing name can also offer a sense of belonging
"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.
Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point," she said.
But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.
"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."
But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.
"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.
Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.
"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."
That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message" and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.
Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.
Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."
But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.
Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.
For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.
"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."
Edited by: Richard Connor

title: Ski Aggu: Rapper will Handys bei Konzerten verbannen
content_c:
Deutscher Rapper Ski Aggu will Handys von seinen Konzerten verbannen
Rapper Ski Aggu, 28, möchte auf seiner kommenden Tour keine Smartphones im Publikum sehen. Als selbst »handysüchtige Person sage ich, dass wir uns zu unserem Glück zwingen müssen, indem wir Handys auf dem Konzert verbieten«, sagte der Berliner der Nachrichtenagentur dpa. Die Leute hätten wieder Lust auf einen Ort, an dem sie einfach abschalten könnten – sowohl selbst als auch ihre Handys, findet der Künstler, der bürgerlich August Jean Diederich heißt und stets mit Skibrille auftritt. Durch das Verbot würden sie noch mehr im Moment sein und die Erinnerungen im Kopf abspeichern.
Ski Aggu hat vor Kurzem sein neues Album »Ski Aggu Musik« veröffentlicht und geht damit 2027 auf Tour. Im Februar und März spielt er Shows in zehn Städten in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz. Auftakt der »Insider Tour« ist in Rostock.
Ski Aggu setzt beim Handyverbot auf Vertrauen
Prinzipiell habe er nichts gegen Handys im Publikum, erklärte der Rapper nun. Er filme selbst gerne Momente, wenn er auf einer Show sei. »Aber die kollektive Nutzung hat so sehr überhandgenommen, dass die Leute sich wieder nach einem handyfreien Ort sehnen. Genauso ist es ja auch in vielen Nachtclubs.« Das Verbot wolle er auf Vertrauensbasis umsetzen. »Ich denke, dass sich das Publikum daran hält und die Regel respektiert.«
- 
1 Min
- 
2 Min
Auch bei anderen Künstlern sind Smartphones tabu. Fans des US-Sängers Bob Dylan müssen bei Konzerten etwa auf Fotos verzichten. Auch die US-Sängerin Phoebe Bridgers erteilte ein Handyverbot bei ihren Shows. Eine gemeinsame Tour von Rapper RIN und Sänger Schmyt hieß sogar »No Phones Allowed«.
description: Er selbst sei eine »absolut handysüchtige Person«: Der Berliner Rapper Ski Aggu wünscht, dass Fans bei seiner Tour das Handy in der Tasche lassen.

title: Marktbericht: Tech-Ausverkauf drückt auf die Anlegerstimmung
content_c:
DAX dürfte zurückfallen Tech-Ausverkauf drückt auf die Anlegerstimmung
Zum Wochenschluss geraten die Börsen in leichte Turbulenzen: An der Wall Street fallen Tech-Titel weit zurück, auch geopolitische Sorgen wachsen. Wird sich der DAX gegen weitere Kursverluste stemmen?
Der Broker IG Markets taxiert den deutschen Leitindex vor dem Start des Xetra-Handels 0,2 Prozent tiefer auf 25.328 Punkte. Am Donnerstag hatten Sorgen über den Technologiesektor, negativ aufgenommene Konzernbilanzen und ein Anstieg beim Ölpreis den Markt belastet.
Der DAX fiel um 1,1 Prozent auf 25.371 Punkte. Die Nervosität der Anleger steige, kommentierte Andreas Lipkow, Stratege bei CMC Markets. Die Risiken für die kommenden Monate nähmen zu.
Geopolitische Sorgen spielen an den Märkten wieder eine größere Rolle. An den Rohstoffmärkten legen die Ölpreise kräftig zu. Derzeit notieren sie auf dem höchsten Stand seit fünf Monaten. Die Rohöl-Sorte Brent aus der Nordsee verteuerte sich in Asien um 0,5 Prozent auf 113,70 Dollar je Barrel (159 Liter). Das US-Öl WTI notierte 0,6 Prozent fester bei 100,05 Dollar.
Die Anleger fürchten, dass die USA und Israel neue Angriffe auf Iran planen - nach den US-Zwischenwahlen am 3. November, oder schon vorher. Auch Angriffe der Huthi-Rebellen in Saudi-Arabien schürten Ängste vor weiteren Unterbrechungen der Energieversorgung.
Auch die Sorgen, dass der Konflikt im Nahen Osten die Inflation anheizen und die Notenbanken zu weiteren Zinserhöhungen zwingen könnte, belasten die Aktienmärkte.
Die US-Vorgaben fallen schwach aus. Während der US-Standardwerteindex Dow Jones bei 52.867 Punkten etwa auf der Stelle trat, verlor der S&P 500 1,2 Prozent auf 7.663 Zähler. Vor allem Technologiewerte geraten derzeit unter Druck: "Die Begeisterung an den Aktienmärkten über High-Tech hat zuletzt deutliche Dämpfer erhalten. Der jüngste weltweite Ausverkauf zeigt, dass Anleger kritisch hinterfragen, inwieweit die hohen Erwartungen an Künstliche Intelligenz erfüllbar sind", sagte Robert Halver, Marktexperte bei der Baader Bank.
Die aktuellen Quartalszahlen der Facebook-Mutter Meta und die Bilanz von Tesla konnten die Skepsis der Anleger nicht zerstreuen. Beide Tech-Konzerne erlitten am Vortag kräftige Kursverluste. Der technologielastige Nasdaq gab 2,6 Prozent auf 26.008 Stellen nach. "Die Anleger erkennen allmählich, dass es einige Lücken in der KI-Story gibt", sagte Marktstratege Paul Nolte von Murphy & Sylvest.
Der massive Ausverkauf bei US-Technologiewerten und die geopolitischen Spannungen haben auch die asiatischen Aktienmärkte ins Minus gedrückt. In Tokio gab der Nikkei-Index 1,7 Prozent auf 61.825 Punkte nach, und der breiter gefasste Topix notierte 1,8 Prozent niedriger bei 3.924 Zählern.
In China setzten sich die Verluste ebenfalls fort. Die Börse Shanghai verlor 1,5 Prozent auf 3.604 Stellen. Der Index der wichtigsten Unternehmen in Shanghai und Shenzhen fiel um 0,8 Prozent auf 4.003 Punkte.

title: Gipfel des Berliner Prozesses mit Kanzler Merz in Montenegro: Für ein Land könnte der angestrebte Beitritt in die EU bald Wirklichkeit werden
content_c:
Bundeskanzler Merz trifft Balkanstaaten: Geht die EU-Annäherung voran?
22. Oktober 2026
Auf dem Flughafen von Tivat in Montenegro wurde Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz bei seiner Ankunft gleich von zwei Flugzeugen der "Air Montenegro" mit einer klar auflackierten Ansage begrüßt.
"Montenegro - nächstes Mitglied der EU", stand da mit großen blauen Lettern auf dem weißen Rumpf der Passagiermaschinen. Das kleinste der sechs Westbalkan-Länder will 2028 das 28. Mitglied der Europäischen Union werden.
Die EU-Kommission, die in Brüssel die Beitrittsverhandlungen steuert, hält alle Bedingungen für erfüllt. Die Mitgliedsstaaten der EU haben noch kein klares Datum genannt. In den letzten Wochen hat vor allem das Mitgliedsland Kroatien (2013 aufgenommen) noch Bedenken angemeldet.
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz führte beim aktuellen Gipfeltreffen mit den Westbalkan-Staaten in Montenegro zusammen mit seinem Kollegen aus dem Gastgeberland den Vorsitz. Er vermied allerdings, eine konkrete Jahreszahl zu nennen, meinte aber, die EU treibe die Erweiterung um die sechs Westbalkan-Staaten nach langer Flaute wieder ernsthaft voran.
"Montenegro ist fast fertig"
"Wir sind wieder auf Kurs und auf einem guten Weg beim Erweiterungsprozess. Montenegro hat seinen Beitrittsvertrag fast fertig und wir arbeiten alle daran, dass der auf Leistung beruhende Prozess so schnell wie möglich voran geht", sagte Merz im Tagungshotel Sveti Stefan an der malerischen Küste nahe der Stadt Budva.
Der Gastgeber, der Ministerpräsident von Montenegro Milojko Spajic, forderte, die EU müsse genauso geschlossen zum Westbalkan stehen, wie sie es derzeit mit der von Russland angegriffenen Ukraine handhabe.
"Die EU muss die gleiche Klarheit in den Erweiterungsprozess einbringen. Erweiterung bedeutet die Wiedervereinigung unseres Kontinents. Die Ausdehnung von Freiheit, Sicherheit, Chancengleichheit auf die Europäer, die den versprochenen Platz im gemeinsamen Haus noch nicht einnehmen konnten".
Die EU müsse die Stärke haben, in herausfordernden Zeiten historische Entscheidungen zu treffen. Es gehe vor allem um eine Perspektive für die jungen Menschen auf dem Balkan.
Stufenweise gegen den Frust
Die EU-Kommission wird voraussichtlich kommende Woche einen konkreten Zeitplan für künftige Beitritte und Beitrittsverhandlungen für die sechs Westbalkan-Staaten, Montenegro, Serbien, Kosovo, Albanien, Nordmazedonien und Bosnien-Herzegowina veröffentlichten.
Darin wird auch vorgeschlagen, die Bewerber um einen Beitritt stufenweise in den lukrativen Binnenmarkt der EU zu integrieren, auch wenn die volle Mitgliedschaft noch nicht erreicht ist. Dieses stufenweise Vorgehen soll die in einigen Staaten herrschende Frustration über den zähen Beitrittsprozess etwas dämpfen.
In Nordmazedonien zum Beispiel ist die Bevölkerung besonders skeptisch. Nur zwölf Prozent der Menschen glauben laut einer Meinungsumfrage noch an einen EU-Beitritt. Nordmazedonien erfüllt die Kriterien für einen Beitritt schon lange, konnte aber wegen Blockaden aus Griechenland und Bulgariendie eigentlichen Beitrittsverhandlungen nicht beginnen.
"Wir verdienen es schon seit langem, in der EU zu sein, aber unglücklicherweise sind wir wegen einiger künstlicher Hindernisse nicht in der Lage, die Verhandlungen zu starten", kritisiert der Premier von Nordmazedonien Hristijan Mickoski. Er erwarte trotzdem bald sinnvolle Botschaften von der EU.
Die Zeiten seien herausfordernd, so der mazedonische Regierungschef, da könne eine erweiterte EU mit mehr Gewicht helfen. "Vielleicht erleben wir die am meisten herausfordernden Zeiten des Jahrhunderts. Der Krieg in der Ukraine, der Krieg im Iran, eine Krise an den Finanzmärkten, Proteste überall in Europa."
Fällt Albanien zurück?
Neben Mazedonien gilt derzeit Albanien als aussichtsreichster Kandidat für einen Beitritt. Die anhaltenden Proteste gegen die Regierung von Ministerpräsident Edi Rama bremsen aber, wie Rama selbst einräumte.
Dem Berliner Prozess, also dem Treffen der Westbalkan-Länder mit 16 Partnerstaaten aus Europa, kann Rama nicht viel abgewinnen. Er sagte nur grinsend, das sei ein Ritual, das man jedes Jahr veranstalte.
Der Berliner Prozess wurde vor zwölf Jahren von der damaligen Bundeskanzlerin Angela Merkel erfunden, um die sechs Balkan-Staaten miteinander ins Gespräch zu bringen und an die EU heranzuführen. Friedrich Merz erinnerte daran, dass der Berliner Prozess auch dazu dienen soll, andere Spieler wie Russland, China und die USA auf dem Balkan nicht zu einflussreich werden zu lassen.
"Der Westbalkan darf nicht zu einem Ort werden, wo große Mächte um Einfluss ringen", sagte der Kanzler nach den Beratungen in Sveti Stefan. Deshalb müsse der Weg der Erweiterung entschlossen weitergegangen werden. Das sei seine Botschaft.
Bei Serbien erst einmal abwarten
Wenig Chancen auf schnelle Fortschritte bei den Beitrittsgesprächen haben Serbien und Kosovo, die ihren Konflikt um die staatliche Unabhängigkeit der ehemaligen serbischen Provinz nicht begelegt haben. Außerdem protestieren in Serbien seit zwei Jahren Studenten gegen die zunehmend autokratische Regierung, die eher Russland zuneigt.
Die EU wartet erst einmal die Ergebnisse der Wahlen am Sonntag in Serbien ab, bei denen die allmächtig scheinende Partei des bisherigen Präsidenten Alexander Vucic verlieren könnte. Bosnien-Herzegowina wird nach wie vor als nicht funktionierender Staat von der EU angesehen. Voraussetzung für sinnvolle Beitrittsgespräche wären aus Sicht der EU, eine Aussöhnung zwischen den ethnischen Gruppen, Bosniern, Serben und Kroaten.
Berliner Prozess als "Korsett"
Deutschland gebe sich Mühe, die Westbalkan-Staaten im Berliner Prozess anzutreiben, meint die Balkanexpertin Funda Tekin vom Berlin Institut für Europapolitik. Die Durchsetzungsmacht sei allerdings begrenzt, sagt sie im Interview mit der DW.
Der Berliner Prozess sei aber nur Beiwerk, eine Beitrittsgarantie sei damit nicht verbunden. "Das kann Deutschland mit dem Prozess auch nicht erreichen. Regionale Zusammenarbeit ersetzt keinen konkreten Fortschritt auf dem Weg zur Mitgliedschaft", so die Balkanexpertin.
Entscheidend sei die finanzielle Unterstützung durch alle 28 Mitgliedsstaaten der EU, zusätzliche Investitionen und politische Anreize seien nötig. Der Berliner Prozess sei das "Korsett", aber nicht der Kern des Beitrittsverfahrens.
Ukraine als Konkurrenz?
Etwas eifersüchtig blicken die Westbalkan-Staaten auf die Ukraine und Moldau, die in nur vier Jahren Schritte zum Beitritt machen, für die andere Bewerber 20 Jahre gebraucht haben. Der geopolitische Druck, die von Russland angegriffene Ukraine schnell aufzunehmen, sei groß, analysiert Funda Tekin vom Berliner Institut für Europapolitik.
Aber die Kriterien, die für den Balkan gelten, müssten auch für die Ukraine gelten, um politische Frustration zu vermeiden. Der deutsche Vorschlag, der Ukraine deshalb erst einmal eine teilweise Mitgliedschaft vor allem auf ökonomischem Gebiet anzubieten, sei richtig, so die Balkan-Expertin. Die Ukraine bleibe ein Sonderfall, bei dem es flexible Lösungen brauche.

title: Україна під атакою реактивних дронів РФ: під прицілом захід, стались вибухи — де загроза (оновлено)
content_c:
Україна під атакою реактивних дронів РФ: під прицілом захід, стались вибухи — де загроза (оновлено)
Мешканців областей, де оголошено повітряну тривогу, закликають перебувати в укриттях і не ігнорувати сигнали небезпеки.
Від самісінького ранку 23 жовтня армія РФ продовжує атакувати Україну реактивними БпЛА. Дрони фіксують одразу в кількох областях, зокрема на заході країни.
Що відомо про рух ударних безпілотників — читайте у матеріалі ТСН.ua.
Протягом ночі росіяни атакували різні регіони України безпілотниками. На ранок обстріл триває. У небі фіксують близько десяти БпЛА.
Нічна атака — що відомо
Зранку Повітряні сили повідомили, що від вечора 22 жовтня Росія запустила 176 ударних БпЛА типу Shahed (92 — реактивні), «Гербера», дрони-імітатори типу «Пародія». Безпілотник летіли із семи напрямків: Брянська, Шаталово, Орла, Курська, Приморсько-Ахтарська, Донецька і території Криму.
Станом на 08:00, було збито/подавлено 140 дронів, з яких 68 — реактивні. Втім, зафіксовано влучання на 19 локаціях, а падіння уламків — на 13 локаціях.
Вранішня атака БпЛА
З мапи тривог видно, що станом на 08:14 безпілотники фіксують на заході — у небі Волині і Рівненщини, а також у кількох районах Львівської та Івано-Франківської областей. Зокрема, реактивний БпЛА — над Львовом.
За Повітряні сили ЗСУ, повідомляють про рух дронів на Чернігівщині: їх фіксують у районі Добрянки. Цілі рухаються південно-західним курсом. Також реактивні БпЛА пролітають повз Славутич у напрямку Київської області.
Зауважимо, монітори повідомляли, що від 4 ранку було здійснено пуски близько 30 груп БпЛА з північного напрямку. За даними Повітряних сил, станом на 07:15 нові реактивні дрони рухаються через зону відчуження Чорнобильської АЕС у західному напрямку. Зокрема, на заході цілі фіксують на Рівненщині, Волині, а також у частині Хмельниччини і Буковини.
Де лунають вибухи
Після 07:00 нові вибухи сколихнули Луцьк. В обласному центрі від 06:32 лунають сирени. «Жовту» тривогу оголосили через загрозу дронів, які летять на місто.
За даними кореспондентів ТСН.ua, у частині міста зникло світло після нових вибухів.
Загроза нових атак
Військовий експерт Олег Жданов попередив, що Росія готує нову балістику, бо намагається використовувати ці ракети як один із найефективніших інструментів тиску. З його слів, ворог продовжить бити по українській енергетичній інфраструктурі. Окрему загрозу становлять спроби Росії збільшити дальність балістичних ракет «Іскандер».
Водночас у ЗСУ попереджають про загрозу для заходу та центру України. Росія випробовує нові реактивні дрони для атак на ці регіони. Днями вони пролетіли рекордні 880 кілометрів і дісталися Львівщини та Волині.

title: Зірка "Бонда" не може грати і читати. Що у неї з очима
content_c:
Зірка "Бонда" не може грати і читати. Що у неї з очима
  - Author, Флоренс Фрімен
- Published
- Час прочитання: 3 хв
Володарка Оскару, акторка Джуді Денч розповіла, що через проблеми із зором вона не може ні виступати на сцені, ні читати, навіть через десять років після встановлення діагнозу.
У 2012 році у Денч діагностували вікову макулярну дегенерацію (ВМД) – стан, який впливає на її зір і, через який їй важко навіть розпізнавати обличчя.
В інтерв'ю BBC Radio 4, акторка розповіла: "Я більше не можу бути на сцені. Я більше не можу грати у виставах. Я більше не можу зніматися у фільмах. Я більше не можу читати".
Вона також розповіла, як через її стан іноді стаються незручні моменти, коли вона підходить не до тих людей "і майже обіймає їх", перш ніж усвідомлює, що це помилка.
Коли Джуді Денч, якій 91 рік, запитали про старіння, вона відповіла: "Мені нічого сказати. Я не надто багато про це думаю".
Вона насолоджується результатами своєї кар'єри, що триває понад сім десятиліть, і є однією із найвідоміших британських акторок, маючи за плечима роботи в театрі, на телебаченні та в кіно.
Вона отримала премію "Оскар" за найкращу жіночу роль другого плану у фільмі "Закоханий Шекспір", де вона грала королеву Єлизавети I.
Також вона здобула міжнародне визнання за роль "М", боса Джеймса Бонда.
Вона дебютувала в цій ролі у фільмі "Золоте око" у 1995 році, ставши першою жінкою, яка зіграла керівницю британської розвідки MI6.
Втрата зору дедалі більше впливає на її працездатність. Ще раніше акторка розповідала про труднощі із зором на знімальних майданчиках та з запам'ятовуванням сценаріїв.
Попри стан, вона продовжує публічно виступати та відкрито говорити про адаптацію до життя з погіршенням зору, заявляючи, що "радіо завжди було для мене важливим".
Під час інтерв'ю Денч згадала, як її запросив на обід колишній шеф MI6 сер Девід Спеддінг, описавши цей досвід як "дуже захопливий".
Коли вона запитала, куди її водій має її підвезти, їй відповіли: "Ні, ні, ми надішлемо вам машину, ми приїдемо і заберемо вас".
Однак вона прибула приблизно на 20 хвилин пізніше, оскільки водій намагався знайти її будинок. "Я сказала: "Вибачте, що так запізнилася, бо ваш водій не зміг знайти мій будинок". Мені дуже сподобалося".
На запитання, чи має вона якусь думку щодо того, хто має зіграти наступного Бонда, вона просто відповіла "ні".

title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
content_c:
Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
- Published
Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said, after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.
Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russian targets in Ukraine and protect itself from attacks.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
- Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? 
  - Published15 October
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.
The networks use 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.
Modern warfare often relies on the use of high-speed internet to effectively operate drones.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.
He told a news conference that the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."
He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."
The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.
The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.
The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.
BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.
Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting the US military may therefore be behind the restrictions.
The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.
  - Published15 October
description: Ukraine relies on Starlink for a range of military uses - its owner Elon Musk has repeatedly denied restricting access.

title: Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
content_c:
Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
- Published
The energy minister has insisted she backs Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms after she made what she described as a "light-hearted remark".
Miatta Fahnbulleh was repeatedly asked in an interview on Wednesday whether she supported the government's plans to increase the time it takes for migrants to gain permanent UK residency, but refused to.
Referring to that exchange, she joked to reporters on Thursday that she did not explicitly answer the question because she had told herself she would "never lie".
In a later statement, she said: "Today I made what was meant to be a light-hearted self-deprecating remark. I didn't get it right and it hasn't come off as I intended."
She added: "I fully support our home secretary and the government's position on migration reform."
Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.
The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years.
Mahmood told Labour Party conference in September the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".
But a significant number of Labour MPs and trade unions want her to water down the proposed policy.
Downing Street has repeatedly insisted that Mahmood is considering responses to a consultation exercise before finalising the reforms.
On Wednesday, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to make sure we get this right."
Asked earlier on the same day on Sky News, whether she backed the proposed reforms, Fahnbulleh said: "We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution."
She was pressed several more times on the issue, saying the government was consulting on the proposals and would "will come out with the measures that we take forward".
At a lunch with political reporters on Thursday, Fahnbulleh said: "I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge [on Sky] yesterday, but nevermind."
In her later statement, she said this was a joke and suggested it was not intended to show she did not support Mahmood's reforms.
"As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship," Fahnbulleh said.
It comes after another Cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, criticised the proposed changes ahead of Labour's conference in Liverpool.
Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.
She later denied there was a split within the heart of government over the issue.

- Mahmood signals rethink on migrants' right to remain 
  - Published28 September

  - Published28 September

  - Published26 September

title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
content_c:
Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
- Published
Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.
The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.
The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.
Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.
Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.
Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.
HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year.
"It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.
However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said.
"Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said.
"It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.
Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".
"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.
Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.
AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.
Barclays also revealed it made £2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.
Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.
"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.
"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.
"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."
Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.
Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".
"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.
Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further £1.1bn of savings in 2027.

title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
content_c:
When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.
But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.
This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.
“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”
The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.
The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.
The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.
Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”
Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.
Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.
“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”
For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.
Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.
“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”
The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.
But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.
Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.
“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”
She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.
“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”
Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.
“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”
During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.
For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.
“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

content:
When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.
But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.
This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.
“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”
The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.
The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.
The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.
Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”
Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.
Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.
“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”

But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.

If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.
“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”

title: ‘No indications’ PHP code flaw has led to government systems being hacked, cyber security official says – as it happened
content_c:
Cyber security official says there are 'no indications' PHP code flaw has led to government computer systems being hacked
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
[This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
We’re in an era now of digital dependency, coupled with heightened cyber threat, coupled with increasing capability, which means all organisations are going to likely have to revisit their risk assumptions and work out how they are able to invest in technology to be able to meet the contemporary era.
Whitehouse said there were “no indications” that the PHP flaw now being fixed had been successfully exploited by hackers.
He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
A UK cyber security official has said that there are “no indications” that the PHP computer coding flaw, that has led to 32 government websites being taken down, has been successfully exploited by hackers. (See 4.46pm.)
MPs pay tribute to Diane Abbott as they debate black history month
MPs debated black history month earlier today. Politicians are often fairly unpleasant to their opponents, but there was a surprise moment near the start of the debate when Joy Morrissey, the Tory spokesperson for women and equalities (and not someone known for being particularly woke or leftwing), paid a moving tribute to the veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott. Morrissey said:
In 1987, the very same year black history month began here, a young woman from Paddington walked into the House of Commons as Britain’s first black female MP. Today, she is the mother of the House.
When she arrived, there were only 41 women in the entire Commons. She was told in a hundred ways that she didn’t belong. She stayed anyway.
For nearly four decades, she has represented the people of Hackney, championed black children in London schools, and chaired parliamentary groups on West Indian and sickle cell disease.
She has faced more abuse than almost any politician of her generation, and she has never stopped turning up.
You don’t have to share her political her politics to recognise what her presence meant. For millions of black Britons, especially black girls, she was proof that the doors of power could open and that someone who looked like them could walk through.
Florence Eshalomi, the communities minister, opened the debate, and she also paid tribute to Abbott. She said she remembered when Abbott was elected in 1987, along with Paul Boateng and Bernie Grant. They were the first black MPs. Eshalomi said:
I was just six years old when [Abbott] was elected, and I remember that quiet hope I felt in watching TV and seeing her in parliament to see that, yes, a black woman can have that voice and that we don’t have to stand by when decisions are made to us and not by us. That gave me the confidence to stand for public office as a local councillor in the borough where I grew up, and later for the London assembly.
Voters significantly more likely to back progressive coalition led by Burnham than Tory/Reform UK one, poll suggests
YouGov has published some interesting polling on what voters think about various coalition options. Here are some of the key points.
Voters are significantly more likely to support a progressive coalition than a rightwing coalition. The most popular coalition option polled was a Labour/Lib Dem one, with Andy Burnham as PM. Some 42% of people would support that. Other progressive options, with Burnham as PM, would get the support of more than a third of voters. But only a quarter of voters would back a Conservative/Reform UK coalition, with a Kemi Badenoch-led version only marginally more popular than a Nigel Farage-led one.
Conservative supporters would rather see the party go into coalition with the Liberal Democrats than with Reform UK. In its write-up, YouGov says:
Most current Conservative supporters would support either arrangement, though more are in favour of the party forming a coalition with the Lib Dems (68%) than Reform (60%), and with at least 28% opposed to either coalition. Lib Dem supporters do not return the favour, with 58% of those currently intending to vote for the party opposed to a repeat of the Cameron-Clegg government, although 36% are in favour.
This is interesting because, on immigration, Brexit, and the European convention on human rights, Badenoch has shifted her party to a position where its policies are near identical to Reform UK’s. Recently there have been signs she has started to steer back the other way.
Most Conservative supporters would not be in favour of a coalition with Reform UK, with Nigel Farage as PM, if the two parties combined could form a majority government. In December last year Conservative supporters (defined as people who voted Tory in 2024) were narrowly in favour of this option. They would still favour a Conservative-Reform UK coalition if Badenoch were PM, but by a narrower margin than last year. YouGov says:
Britons have become less inclined towards a Farage-led Reform-Tory coalition, with net support for such a government falling from -27 to -41 since last December. This includes 2024 Conservative voters going from being effectively divided on the question (+5) to being clearly opposed (-13).
Conservative voters have also become less receptive to a Badenoch-led Tory-Reform coalition, with net support falling 15 points since the end of last year to +23, even if those who voted Reform at the last election have become more open to the idea, with net support doubling to +22.
Fahnbulleh says ministers won't 'faff around' in getting rid of gas standing charges, implying decision coming in budget
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has heightened speculation that a government announcement about getting rid of the standing charges on gas bills will come in the budget on Wednesday next week.
Andy Burnham implied this strongly yesterday when he said he had asked John Healey, the chancellor, and Fahnbulleh to look at this idea and to report back to MPs “at the earliest opportunity”. The “earliest opportunity” is Wednesday next week, because that will be the first time either of those two MPs gets to address the Commons.
Today, speaking to a press gallery lunch, Fahnbulleh confirmed that an announcement is likely very soon. She said Burnham had made it clear the government “can’t faff around”.
She explained:
I love working with him because Andy is very clear … in his mind about the sorts of things that he wants us to do, and he’s really impatient with change.
And so, if you ask the department, ‘Oh, you know, standing charge reform’, they’re like, ‘Oh, we’d have to consult. This is a 10-year proposition’. And Andy’s like, ‘I want you and John to look at it and come back with an answer’. So we’re looking at the options.
Fahnbulleh said getting rid of standing charges would be popular.
The thing I do know is that the public absolutely hates standing charges, and it’s a control question. People just find that really egregious, and their ability to manage their energy bills by deciding how much they want to use on their terms is essentially taken away from them. So, even shifting it into the unit rate gives people that agency.
She said modelling suggested the move could reduce the bills of “a big stack of low-income through to middle-income households”.
She went on:
There are some people that will be impacted negatively because they are essentially low-income, high users, and so you need to think about mitigations. But we’re looking at all the options.
But the thing that he is very clear on is we can’t faff around. We need to get on with this. So watch this space.
According to research by Nesta, a research foundation, 64% of households would benefit if the government got rid of the standing charge and instead loaded those costs onto the unit charge. But households using large amounts of gas would pay more.
Our analysis shows that, on its own, abolishing the gas standing charge would save the typical dual fuel household £27 per year, and that 64% of dual fuel households will be better off under this policy.
Because the distribution of gas consumption is skewed by a small number of (predominantly wealthy) households, the average and median household are quite a way apart. The threshold at which this policy would start to increase bills is around 12,400 kWh, but a majority of homes (64%) use less gas than this. This is why the typical household (using only 9,500 kWh of gas) would expect to save around £27 per year under this policy.
TDCV stands for typical domestic consumption values – a figure for how much gas and electricity an average household is using at any point.
Burnham has flu jab, as NHS encourages those eligible for free injection to get one
Andy Burnham has had his flu jab. He has posted about it on Instagram, and at the same time the Department of Health and Social Care is launching a publicity campaign to encourage people eligible for a free jab to get one.
James Frith, a health minister, said:
Vaccines save lives. It has never been easier to find out if you are eligible and get vaccinated, helping protect yourself and reduce pressure on the NHS during the winter season.
Eligibility is focused on those most vulnerable - from young children to older adults and people with long-term health conditions - so if you are eligible, please come forward this winter.
In England, most children under 17 are eligible for a free flu jab, as well as people over 65, people with some long-term health conditions, pregnant women, carers and people living in a care home, people living with someone with a weakened immune system, homeless people and frontline health and care workers.
The latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping talking about whether or not the government will allow the Rosebank oilfield development to go ahead, after the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield was approved yesterday.
Starmer granted core participant status in grooming gangs inquiry
Keir Starmer may be summoned to give evidence at the grooming gangs inquiry, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The former prime minister, who ordered the probe last year, has been listed as a core participant for the inquiry’s hearings which are due to begin in December.
This means he is among people, groups and organisations formally granted special status by the chairwoman under public inquiry rules, giving him rights to participate in the investigation.
While this does not automatically mean he will be required to give evidence, many core participants are asked or compelled to do so.
Victims and their families, charities, whistleblowers, police chiefs and government departments are among those also listed as core participants.
The scandal-hit probe is looking at how grooming gangs operated in England and Wales and the actions of police, councils, health and social care services, schools and other public bodies.
An inquiry spokesman said the decision on core participant status “considers whether a person played, or may have played, a direct and significant role in relation to the matters to which the inquiry relates, whether they have a significant interest in an important aspect of the matters to which the inquiry relates, or whether the person may be subject to explicit or significant criticism during the inquiry proceedings or in the report, or in any interim report”, adding: “Nobody is beyond examination or transparency, and that the inquiry is following the evidence, wherever it leads.”
Starmer was prime minister when the grooming gangs inquiry was announced last year. But he was also director of public prosecutions from 2008 to 2013, at a time when the CPS was being accused of being too reluctant to prosecute in many cases of alleged child sexual abuse. As DPP, Starmer set out to change this – ordering prosecutors to be more sympathetic to victims, and less inclined to disbelieve them or to drop cases because victims might not make compelling witnesses.
According to Christopher Hope from GB News, Kemi Badenoch is unhappy about Andy Burnham going on Gogglebox (see 2.35pm) – but only because she wants an invite too! Hope says:
A political row has broken out over Andy Burnham’s decision to go on Channel 4’s programme ‘Gogglebox’. A Tory source tells me that Kemi Badenoch should be invited on to the show. One says: “It’s Channel 4’s job to ensure political balance.”

He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
Burnham to appear on Gogglebox with Steve Rotheram
Kemi Badenoch has been routinely complaining about Andy Burnham spending time on supposedly trivial things, like discussing how he makes his tea in a summer Q&A, or doing a social media video about pork scratchings. So God know what she is going to say when she finds out he’s on Gogglebox tomorrow night.
The PM will be appearing on the show tomorrow night for a Gogglebox for Stand Up To Cancer special. He will be on the sofa with his friend Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor.
As Max Goldbart writes in an article for Deadline, there is some precedent for his appearance.
Seen as something of an everyman, Burnham will now get the chance to broadcast his thoughts on the week’s TV to millions. An Instagram reel teasing his appearance shows him offering crisps and beer to Rotheram.
Burnham is the first prime minister to appear on Gogglebox. Jeremy Corbyn, who was leader of the opposition at the time, came on the show a decade ago, while former PM Boris Johnson’s father Stanley Johnson appeared two years later.
“Nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing – the equivalent of travelling between London and Singapore – will be completed this year,” the Department for Transportis saying. It says councils in England are doing 10% more resurfacing than last year, because they are getting more government funding.
Mahmood condemned by Unison for refusing to let care worker attend private meeting about her 'nasty' proposed ILR changes
Andrea Egan, the Unison general secretary, has criticised Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, for not letting her bring a care worker to a meeting to discuss Mahmood’s plans to tighten the permanent residency rules for foreign workers.
Egan described the proposals as “nasty”, and said Mahmood’s failure to engage with people affected by the rules was “totally unacceptable”.
The Unison leader was commenting in a post on social media that referenced a story by Arj Singh for the i, which said talks between Mahmood and Unison “broke down after the home secretary refused to allow a migrant care worker to attend the meeting”. Singh said:
The meeting was cancelled by Unison after Mahmood refused Egan’s late request to bring a migrant care worker who will be affected by the “earned settlement” changes, The i Paper understands.
Mahmood is under pressure to water down her proposals, particularly those relating to care workers, and Unison, which represents many workers in the care sector, has campaigned particularly forcefully against the plan.
In her social media posts, Egan said:
Shabana Mahmood’s failure to engage properly with the migrant workers whose lives her nasty proposals will devastate is totally unacceptable.
These are brilliant, committed workers who hold our public services together. UNISON won’t tolerate them being attacked and ignored.
I’ve changed UNISON’s political approach to put members first. That includes taking members with me to government meetings.
Engaging directly with workers should be standard for Labour cabinet ministers, not something they run away from.
In his report, Singh says:
The care worker who Egan wanted to bring to the meeting has completed an NVQ level 3 and is set to do further qualifications so that he can develop his career in the sector, and was planning to tell Mahmood about why he and many other Unison members had chosen to work in the sector.
Singh quotes a Home Office source as saying that Egan had been invited to a private meeting with Mahmood and that it was Unison that chose to cancel it. The source also said that it would be wrong for Mahmood to prioritise the views of just one care worker when 200,000 responses to the government’s consultation were being considered.
In a social media post commenting on the same story, the Labour MP John McDonnell said:
The work visa issue is causing totally unnecessary division in the Labour Party at a time when the new leader is settling himself into the job. Listening to numerous workers employed on work visas in the care sector has been essential in gaining an understanding of what they face and the effect on our public services of the proposed rule changes. All Unison wanted was to ensure the home secretary had the opportunity to appreciate fully the concerns of the people who will be affected by her proposals. I urge her to think again on this decision not to meet.
32 UK government services offline while work carried out to sort out PHP programming flaw, minister says
Some 32 government services are offline and four are partially unavailable while work is carried out to address potential cybersecurity issues, a minister has said.
As the Press Association reports, organisations around the world have been scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites.
Downing Street on Thursday said no large UK public-facing critical services have been affected, but some “limited” government websites have gone dark while issues are resolved. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) experts are working with OpenAI, whose technology was used to discover the vulnerabilities, and partners around the globe to address potential problems, a No 10 spokesperson said.
In the House of Lords, Liz Lloyd, the tech minister, said:
The information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable.
Lloyd said that “has largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied”.
The No 10 spokesperson told reporters:
Work has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.
Here is our story about the global impact of the problems identified in the PHP programming language. It’s by Robert Booth and Aisha Down.
Steve Witkoff wrong about Putin being a 'humanitarian', says No 10
Yesterday Steve Witkoff, the property developer appointed by Donald Trump as his lead foreign policy envoy, described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”. Andrew Roth has more about that here, in a piece pointing out that this is an extraordinary lie.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, was giving interviews this morning. Asked if he agreed with Witkoff’s description on LBC, he was reassuringly blunt. He replied:
No, we don’t.
We see him as somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil.
So we simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.
In contrast, we are crystal clear that we stand foursquare behind Volodymyr Zelensky and the people of Ukraine in their battle for freedom.
At the No 10 lobby briefing, a No 10 spokesperson also argued that Witkoff had got it wrong. Asked about Witkoff’s comment, the spokesperson said:
We do not recognise that characterisation … Putin has killed thousands of people, Ukrainians and his own. He’s starving children and the elderly of heat and warmth and destroying critical national infrastructure.
Tories claim crime figures 'spiralling out of control' - and why the data doesn't back this up
The Conservative party seems to have missed the bit in the ONS report on the crime figures where it said “crime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years”. (See 9.54am.) Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued a statement saying:
Crime is spiralling out of control under Labour. Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it. This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.
The Tories justify this claim by looking at the ONS report and picking out all the worst bits (a technique not unfamiliar in the world of journalism). Their briefing highlights four figures in particular. Here is an extract.
Sexual offences have reached the highest level on record under Labour, with the police now logging around 600 of them every single day. Police in England and Wales recorded 218,994 sexual offences in the year to June 2026, the highest annual total since the series began in 2002-03 …
Police are recording more rapes of women than at any point since records began, at a rate of around 142 every day. There were 51,731 recorded rapes of women aged 16 or over in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2004-05 …
More people are being caught carrying knives and blades than at any point since records began. Police recorded 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2008-09 …
Thefts and robberies from shops have reached a record high under Labour, with more than 1,500 recorded every single day. Police recorded 519,516 shoplifting offences and 31,089 robberies of business property in the year to June 2026, a combined 550,605 and the highest total since the series began in 2002-03.
But these claims are highly selective – to the point of being misleading.
On sexual offences, and rape, the ONS report points out that much of the increase over time is due to more offences being recorded, and not necessarily more of them taking place. It says “there has been a general increase in police recorded sexual offences over the last decade, largely because of improvements in police recording practices”. And it includes a specific warning about drawing the wrong conclusions from the figures.
Police recorded sexual offences are not a good indicator of trends over time. Improvements in police recording practices, the introduction of new offences, and increased reporting by victims have contributed to the level of offences in recent years.
On knives, while more people may be carrying them, the Tories have ignored the figures suggesting fewer criminals are actually using them. The ONS says:
Knife-enabled crime recorded by the police decreased by 6% in year ending (YE) June 2026 (to 48,615 offences), compared with YE June 2025 (51,567 offences). Levels remained 12% lower than YE March 2020 (55,170 offences).
And, on shoplifting, the Tories are again presenting the data in a misleading way. The ONS says:
Following a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in YE June 2026 when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences).
The Tories have justified their “record high” claim by combining the shoplifing figures with the figures for robberies from business properties. They describe this as “shop crime” – even though many business properties are not shops. And the ONS has a caveat about these figures too.
The number of robbery of personal property offences fell by 7% (to 57,193 offences) compared with the previous year, however, overall robbery increased by 10% (to 88,282 offences) mainly because of improvements to recording practices for robbery of business property.
And the ONS says, with shoplifting, more offences are also now being recorded than in the past.
Recent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers. Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.
