title: Friday briefing: How a leaderless student group is challenging power in Serbia
content_c:
Good morning. As waves of youth-led protests swell across Europe, prompted by the cost of living, unaffordable housing and education standards, in Serbia the younger generation is taking on the apparatus of the state itself.
In tight-run parliamentary elections this Sunday, the country’s most consequential political movement in decades, Student List, is challenging former Slobodan Milošević henchman Aleksandar Vučić and his 12-year domination of Serbian politics.
Two years on from a singular national tragedy that galvanised public anger at state cover-ups and corruption, gen Z have channelled their energy and fury into a bold experiment in direct democracy, creating a genuinely leaderless, grassroots movement that is firing up disaffected voters across the country.
I spoke to Julian Borger, our senior international correspondent, who has just returned from Belgrade, about their hopes of emulating the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary and the potential for a democratic domino through central Europe. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK news | Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
- 
  Ukraine | Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations.
- 
  UK politics | Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader.
- 
  Europe news | Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years.
- 
  Energy | Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.
In depth: ‘The essence of our movement is direct democracy’
It was, one Serbian student told me, “the drop that overflowed the glass”. On 1 November 2024, the collapse of a concrete canopy at the railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second largest city, killed 16 people. The youngest was a six-year-old girl, Sara Firic, who was sitting on a bench with her grandfather and older sister. The Serbian Times reported they were still holding hands when their bodies were dug out of the rubble.
In the aftermath of the disaster, student-led protests developed organically, with demonstrators blocking a nearby crossroads for the same number of minutes as lives lost. As details emerged of botched refurbishment work carried out in what critics described as a corrupt deal with a Chinese consortium, the anger mounted. Ongoing protests were brutally suppressed and Vučić himself branded demonstrators western-backed “terrorists”.
Two years later, that single tragedy has sparked a mass movement for accountability and inclusive democracy to counter the creeping authoritarianism of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS).
“There was a deep well of public discontent, and the students were inspirational in keeping the protest movement going,” says Julian.
Vučić expected the protesters to dissipate – instead, the mounting pressure forced the president to resign and call a snap parliamentary election, as he endeavours to consolidate his 12 years in power in a Putin-inspired switch to become prime minister.
In response, the student movement is fielding a list of 250 candidates of its own, mainly locally respected academics but also actors, musicians and farmers, with each candidate approved by citizens’ assembly.
Some polling suggests that Student List is edging ahead; others that the SNS is consolidating support. Julian tells me he left Belgrade with the sense that anything could happen on Sunday.
How did a student network put together an election campaign?
The Serbian student I spoke to is buzzing ahead of Sunday’s vote: “We’re really excited,” he tells me over the phone from the Serbian capital. “We hope we win.” He is studying for a masters in dramatic arts at the University of Belgrade, and asks not to be named in accordance with the leader-less structure of his movement.
He talks me through the “big collective effort”, including collecting canvas data door to door, and the “A student in every village” programme targeting Vučić’s base of rural voters, all coordinated by democratic citizens’ assembly. The thinking is that a higher turnout of disaffected voters will favour Student List.
Julian encapsulates the Student List movement as “a bold democratic experiment”, and that is how my student describes it: “The essence of our movement is direct democracy. This collective effort is about making people feel part of the decision-making, not just spectators.”
When Julian joined Student List volunteers canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb, they were met with overwhelmingly positive reactions – “the response was ‘bring it on’” – though he caveats that opinion in outlying suburbs varies from those of the urban intelligentsia and others in more rural settings.
“People were saying to the volunteers, ‘Take my contact and tell me anything I can do on election day.’ There’s a feeling of now or never.”
The demands of the student movement are focused on governance, Julian tells me, and their slogan, “Serbia or mafia?”, highlights repeated allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, something the government denies. “Student List wants a rules-based order that conforms with the constitution on paper, not the system of classic crony capitalism that Vučić has established, where everything depends on your link to the SNS.”
How has the Vučić regime fought back?
Julian says Vučić is plainly taking the Student List threat seriously. He made 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.
But the elections are happening in a context of growing repression: Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years. And only last week, the Guardian revealed that Vučić intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected landmark in Belgrade for a Trump tower, another spur for recent protests.
A September survey for Serbian pro-democracy group the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) found no negative coverage of the ruling majority on the country’s television channels, compared with 37% of the time for the opposition.
Student List has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping overseas polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to Julian’s request to comment.
Meanwhile the digital rights group SHARE Foundation found that members of the student movement had been targeted by advanced spyware, while Reuters this week reported on intimidation and beating of protesters by police.
What is the likely aftermath of Sunday’s elections?
With preliminary results expected in the early hours of Monday morning, a fundamental problem for the country is that neither side sees the other as legitimate, says Julian. “So in the aftermath of the election, barring a really clear decision, it will be disputed one way or another.”
Indeed, the European Council on Foreign Relations has warned of further street protests and possible violent repression, depending on the outcome and the margin of victory.
Big questions remain around how Student List would configure themselves as a government. Reforming the state and economy after more than a decade of highly centralised SNS control will be immensely challenging. So far their policy platform has been decided by full general assembly, and divisive issues such as future relations with Kosovo or Russia, and stance on EU membership, have been played down.
Although Serbia is an EU-candidate country, public opinion on accession is split, and the SNS has counter-balanced relationships with the US, Russia and China, particularly after the Trump administration opened dialogue on energy and technology with them earlier this year.
A Student List win would throw this geopolitical balancing act, which protesters argue brings little benefit to the people of Serbia, up in the air and potentially bring the country closer to Europe. And a contested Vučić victory would challenge the EU on whether to freeze diplomacy and funding to the country.
The student organiser I spoke with is clear that regime change is just the beginning: “Once we remove the regime, the big debate starts in Serbia about what we should do next. Should we join the EU? What about foreign policy? How are we going to democratise the country? There’s a lot that’s not working because of corruption. But right now we’re focused on these elections.”

title: 96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
content_c:
96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse
October 22, 2026
Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.
In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.
Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.
Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.
"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
What are the threats to the reefs?
Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).
Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.
This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.
Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.
When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.
Can the reefs still be saved?
"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.
"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.
"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.
IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."
"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.
In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.
Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.
Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.
"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
What are the threats to the reefs?
Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).
Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.
This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.
Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.
When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.
Can the reefs still be saved?
"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.
"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.
"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.
IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."
"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

title: Übung mit scharfen Granaten löste tödlichen Brand aus
content_c:
Militärstützpunkt in Kanada Übung mit scharfen Granaten löste tödlichen Brand aus
Der verheerende Buschbrand auf einem kanadischen Militärstützpunkt, bei dem am Samstag mindestens vier Menschen getötet wurden, ist nach Angaben des Militärs durch eine Übung mit scharfen Granaten ausgelöst worden. »Das Feuer brach auf dem Schießplatz für automatische Granatwerfer aus«, sagte Brigadegeneralin Vanessa Hanrahan am Donnerstag (Ortszeit).
Es sei als Folge eines routinemäßigen militärischen Trainings entstanden, das zu diesem Zeitpunkt dort stattgefunden habe. Derzeit würden noch 27 Verletzte in Krankenhäusern behandelt, mehrere von ihnen befänden sich in einem kritischen Zustand. Zuvor waren offiziellen Angaben zufolge 39 Verletzte gemeldet worden.
Das Feuer war am Samstagnachmittag auf dem Stützpunkt Wainwright ausgebrochen und durch starken Wind zu einer Feuerwand angefacht worden. Der Wind hatte die Flammen mit einer Geschwindigkeit von bis zu 96 Kilometern pro Stunde vorangetrieben und Angehörige der kanadischen Streitkräfte eingekesselt.
Erinnerung an die verstorbenen Soldaten am Stützpunkt Wainwright (20. Oktober)
Foto: Christopher Katsarov / The Canadian Press / AP
Generalmajor Wade Rutland sagte, dass Soldaten während einer Übung im Freien von den Flammen überrascht worden seien. Es habe sich auf dem Gelände des Stützpunktes über Brandschutzstreifen hinweg ausgebreitet. Schließlich sei es in Zusammenarbeit mit den Einsatzkräften vor Ort eingedämmt worden.
Premierminister Carney bezeichnete den Brand auf dem Stützpunkt Wainwright mit mindestens vier Todesopfern und Dutzenden Verletzten als »eine der schlimmsten Tragödien« der kanadischen Streitkräfte auf Landesboden in Friedenszeiten.
Die Regierungschefin des Bundesstaats Alberta, Danielle Smith, berichtete am Montag, 19 der Verletzten seien in einem »kritischen Zustand«. Acht der Verletzten befanden sich nach Behördenangaben in einem »stabilen« Zustand; zwölf von ihnen wurden wegen leichterer Verletzungen medizinisch behandelt.
Die betroffenen Soldaten bereiteten sich auf einen Einsatz in Lettland vor, der derzeit größten internationalen Militäroperation Kanadas. Premierminister Mark Carney hatte den Brand als eine der schlimmsten Tragödien in Friedenszeiten bezeichnet, die die kanadischen Streitkräfte jemals auf heimischem Boden erlebt haben.

title: Klimawandel: Fast alle Korallenriffe weltweit vom Absterben bedroht
content_c:
Folgen des Klimawandels Fast alle Korallenriffe weltweit vom Absterben bedroht
Korallen bieten im Meer einer großen Artenvielfalt ein Zuhause. Doch die Riffe sind durch die Erhitzung der Meere erheblich gefährdet. Eine Studie zeigt nun das ganze Ausmaß.
Durch den Klimawandel sind in den kommenden 50 Jahren fast alle Korallenriffe vom Absterben bedroht. Das ist das Ergebnis einer Prognose der Weltnaturschutzunion (IUCN), die diese am Rande der derzeit laufenden UN-Artenschutzkonferenz in Armenien vorgestellt hat. Es bestehe für 96 Prozent der Korallenriffe in den Weltmeeren "ein extrem erhöhtes Risiko", dass sie bis 2075 absterben, hieß es in der Analyse.
Für die Bewertung wurden der Zustand und die Entwicklung von Korallenriffen vor den Küsten von mehr als 80 Ländern und Gebieten eingeschätzt. Als Grundlage diente den Wissenschaftlern dafür das "mittlere" Szenario des UN-Klimarats, das bis zum Jahr 2100 eine globale Erwärmung um 2,7 Grad Celsius gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau prognostiziert. Das von der Weltgemeinschaft eigentlich angestrebte Ziel von 1,5 Grad gilt inzwischen als fast nicht mehr erreichbar.
Hitzestress als größte Bedrohung
"Hitzestress infolge des Klimawandels ist weltweit die beständigste Bedrohung, die den Rückgang der Korallenriffe vorantreibt", erklärte die Weltnaturschutzunion. Daneben wurden auch Überfischung, Küstenbebauung, Umweltverschmutzung, Tourismus und durch den Klimawandel immer häufiger auftretende Stürme als schädigende Faktoren genannt.
Korallen bilden natürliche Barrieren gegen Erosion und bieten als Ökosysteme eine große Artenvielfalt. Sie sind jedoch sehr empfindlich gegenüber Temperaturschwankungen. Wird das Wasser zu warm, stoßen sie die Mikroalgen ab, die in ihrem Gewebe leben und sie ernähren. Sie bleichen aus und sterben oft ab. Hitzewellen im Meer treten wegen des Klimawandels immer häufiger auf.
Weltweit erste Untersuchung dieser Art
Betroffen sind demnach unter anderem Teile des Great Barrier Reef vor Australien, des Korallendreiecks im westlichen Pazifik und in Südostasien, des mesoamerikanischen Riffsystems und die Riffe im Roten Meer. Das seien die weltweit größten und artenreichsten Riffe.
Die IUCN ist ein Dachverband zahlreicher Regierungs- und Nichtregierungsorganisationen im Bereich Natur- und Artenschutz. Die nun vorgelegte Analyse war die erste weltweite Untersuchung dieser Art.

title: Зранку РФ атакує обласний центр на заході: лунають сильні вибухи (оновлено)
content_c:
РФ атакувала обласний центр на заході: після серії вибухів зникло світло (оновлено)
Після вранішніх вибухів у частині Луцька зникло електропостачання.
Зрання 23 жовтня у Луцьку прогриміли сильні вибухи. В обласному центрі о 06:32 було оголошено повітряну тривогу, яка тривала дві години.
Що відомо про атаку і її наслідки — читайте у матеріалі ТСН.ua.
На Волині кілька разів оголошували повітряну тривогу через дронову загрозу. Вночі у Луцьку вже було гучно. Нові вибухи сталися о 07:01 та 07:30.
Секретар міськради Андрій Разумовський заявив, що на місто летять БпЛА і закликав містян перебувати в укриттях.
Відключення світла у Луцьку
За даними кореспондентів ТСН.ua, у місті почало зникло світло. Місцеві Телеграм-канали пишуть про пошкодження підстанцій, які живлять Луцьк. Наразі інформації від обленерго немає.
Водночас у мерії повідомили, що в обласному центрі тимчасово не курсують тролейбуси. Рух автобусів відбувається за графіком.
«У зв’язку з відсутністю електроживлення контактної мережі рух тролейбусів у Луцьку тимчасово призупинено», — наголосили у пресслужбі.
Нагадаємо, від самого ранку 23 жовтня Україна перебуває під атакою. Реактивними БпЛА фіксували одразу в кількох областях, зокрема на заході країни: у Волинській, Рівненській, частині Хмедьницької і Чернівецької областей.

title: Зеленский о планах реформировать управление Киевом: "Я хочу создать кабинет"
content_c:
Президент Украины Владимир Зеленский заявил, что проводит консультации по созданию "кабинета", задачей которого будет укрепление власти в Киеве и ускорение решения вопросов безопасности столицы, цитирует его слова "Интерфакс–Украина". Глава государства напомнил, что в связи с этим проводил закрытые встречи с представителями сферы безопасности и бизнеса, с которыми он обсудил усиление города.
"Мой диалог с теми или иными людьми — это укрепление столицы. Попробуй-ка заставить людей создать кабинет, — отметил президент, но о возможном увольнении действующего городского главы Виталия Кличко говорить не стал. — Я хочу создать кабинет, который сможет укрепить мэра, укрепить киевлян, укрепить Киев, а не то, что там кто-то за что-то борется".
Логистика и самоуправление — те вопросы, которыми должны заниматься органы местного самоуправления, подчеркивает Зеленский. Однако он соглашается с тезисом о том, что иногда им может не хватать для этого ресурсов.
В начале октября Зеленский обвинил власти Киева в "почти полном невыполнении необходимых мер" по подготовке к зиме, напомнив, что для города были определены конкретные задачи. Впоследствии он анонсировал решения, которые коснутся изменения системы управления столицей, но идет ли речь об увольнении мэра — не уточнил, вместо этого упрекнув в том, что прифронтовые и приграничные области демонстрируют лучшие показатели выполнения планов, чем Киев.
Кличко ответил. Сначала он предъявил центральной власти обвинения в попытках уничтожить местное самоуправление и заявил, что любые претензии в адрес властей столицы являются безосновательными, а затем, во время отчета в ВР о подготовке к зиме, назвал "шоу" Планы устойчивости, которые в начале года утвердил СНБО, обвинил Банковую в отсутствии защиты энергообъектов и напомнил о блокировании денег громад. А вот об укрытиях и строительстве в Киеве — ни слова.
Директор аналитико-исследовательского центра "Институт города" Александр Сергиенко в материале "Выстоит ли Киев следующей зимой? Под ударами извне и подножками внутри" уже писал, что Совбез установил абсолютно непосильную для столицы сумму, необходимую для реализации Плана устойчивости — 67,5 млрд грн при том, что весь бюджет Киева составляет 106 млрд. Как следствие, городские власти предложили покрыть лишь 20,4 млрд, а остальные деньги взять из квоты Кабмина. Кроме того, в материале "Кто построит укрытия — и кто отвечает за безопасность киевлян?" Сергиенко отмечал, что именно районные госадминистрации не использовали 500 млн, предусмотренных сначала на стационарные укрытия, а потом — на мобильные. Впрочем, в КГВА из-за этого лишь разводят руками, а в КМДА говорят, что эти вопросы не входят в их полномочия.
В целом это не первый случай, когда на фоне энергетического кризиса в Киеве обостряется противостояние между президентом и мэром. Но, как отмечал Сергиенко в статье "Киев под атаками извне и изнутри, или Политические игры на войне", центральная власть уже неоднократно перекладывала ответственность на местную, когда не справлялась со своими же функциями: задача защиты энергогенерации столицы находится в компетенции КГВА, которая подчиняется президенту. К тому же Кличко еще в январе заявлял, что предупреждал тогдашнего премьера Юлию Свириденко об угрозах и рисках, которые могут возникнуть в случае сильных повреждений инфраструктуры столицы из-за российских атак, но не получил никаких предложений в ответ, а через несколько месяцев жаловался на отсутствие помощи в восстановлении ТЭЦ-5.

Попробуй-ка заставить людей создать кабинет, — отметил президент, но о возможном увольнении действующего городского главы Виталия Кличко говорить не стал. — Я хочу создать кабинет, который сможет укрепить мэра, укрепить киевлян, укрепить Киев, а не то, что там кто-то за что-то борется".
Логистика и самоуправление — те вопросы, которыми должны заниматься органы местного самоуправления, подчеркивает Зеленский. Однако он соглашается с тезисом о том, что иногда им может не хватать для этого ресурсов.
В начале октября Зеленский обвинил власти Киева в "почти полном невыполнении необходимых мер" по подготовке к зиме, напомнив, что для города были определены конкретные задачи. Впоследствии он анонсировал решения, которые коснутся изменения системы управления столицей, но идет ли речь об увольнении мэра — не уточнил, вместо этого упрекнув в том, что прифронтовые и приграничные области демонстрируют лучшие показатели выполнения планов, чем Киев.
Кличко ответил. Сначала он предъявил центральной власти обвинения в попытках уничтожить местное самоуправление и заявил, что любые претензии в адрес властей столицы являются безосновательными, а затем, во время отчета в ВР о подготовке к зиме, назвал "шоу" Планы устойчивости, которые в начале года утвердил СНБО, обвинил Банковую в отсутствии защиты энергообъектов и напомнил о блокировании денег громад. А вот об укрытиях и строительстве в Киеве — ни слова.
Директор аналитико-исследовательского центра "Институт города" Александр Сергиенко в материале "Выстоит ли Киев следующей зимой? Под ударами извне и подножками внутри" уже писал, что Совбез установил абсолютно непосильную для столицы сумму, необходимую для реализации Плана устойчивости — 67,5 млрд грн при том, что весь бюджет Киева составляет 106 млрд. Как следствие, городские власти предложили покрыть лишь 20,4 млрд, а остальные деньги взять из квоты Кабмина. Кроме того, в материале "Кто построит укрытия — и кто отвечает за безопасность киевлян?" Сергиенко отмечал, что именно районные госадминистрации не использовали 500 млн, предусмотренных сначала на стационарные укрытия, а потом — на мобильные. Впрочем, в КГВА из-за этого лишь разводят руками, а в КМДА говорят, что эти вопросы не входят в их полномочия.
В целом это не первый случай, когда на фоне энергетического кризиса в Киеве обостряется противостояние между президентом и мэром. Но, как отмечал Сергиенко в статье "Киев под атаками извне и изнутри, или Политические игры на войне", центральная власть уже неоднократно перекладывала ответственность на местную, когда не справлялась со своими же функциями: задача защиты энергогенерации столицы находится в компетенции КГВА, которая подчиняется президенту. К тому же Кличко еще в январе заявлял, что предупреждал тогдашнего премьера Юлию Свириденко об угрозах и рисках, которые могут возникнуть в случае сильных повреждений инфраструктуры столицы из-за российских атак, но не получил никаких предложений в ответ, а через несколько месяцев жаловался на отсутствие помощи в восстановлении ТЭЦ-5.

title: At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
content_c:
At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
- Published
At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.
Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.
In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines in the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post on X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."
More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west.
France's weather service, Météo-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday.
The alert covers Côtes-d'Armor, Finistère, Morbihan, Ille-et-Vilaine and Manche.
Storm Adam had already brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, where at least three people were killed.
Several towns along the Mediterranean coast were cut off by floodwaters, while helicopters were deployed to rescue people stranded on rooftops.
Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva, Valencia, during rescue operations on Monday.
Two other women were confirmed dead over the weekend. One woman's body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a promise that the national government would provide resources to help in reconstruction during a visit to the Valencia region on Tuesday.
The Valencian government approved on Tuesday an aid package of €23.5m (£20m) for those affected by Storm Adam.

title: MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
content_c:
MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
- Published
NHS founder Aneurin "Nye" Bevan was spied on by MI5 for more than 20 years, according to newly released files.
Papers given to the National Archives show he first came to the attention of the Security Service in the 1930s when he was considered a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists.
Monitoring continued after Bevan, from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, became a minister in the post-war Labour government when he drove through the creation of the NHS in the face of opposition from doctors.
At one stage the-then MI5 director general became so concerned about his links to a Russian spy that he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee in No 10 to warn him.
But some in the service questioned why it was taking an interest in him, given everything he did was in the open.
After his death in 1960, one MI5 officer called the content of the file "remarkably tame".
The papers show MI5 first opened a file on Bevan when he was backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in 1933.
One of the first reports included an account of an anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, Canada, which Bevan addressed in 1934.
"Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause," it said.
In 1943, Roger Hollis, future director general, summarised what they knew of Bevan's activities.
In 1933 he said the MP had been "in close touch" with Communist Party of Great Britain general secretary Harry Pollitt and party members who backed his plan to organise "workers' freedom groups" to defend against "capitalists".
Although there was nothing in the files to indicate MI5 tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were watching him at all.
"I do not think that Bevan's activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved," one officer wrote in 1943.
"In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently."
The reporting continued after the war when Bevan was made health minister in Attlee's government.
In 1949 MI5 became increasingly concerned about Bevan's friendship with Wilfred Macartney, "an unsavoury, unscrupulous character" convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.
Recordings of conversations suggested he was passing information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt.
That May the Security Service's chief Sir Percy Sillitoe took evidence to Attlee, who dismissed Macartney's claims as a "tissue of lies" but agreed to warn Bevan about him.
One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Bevan, now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, at London's Polish embassy.
The event "went off very badly", partly because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Bevan's accent, which led to misunderstanding.
"The party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere," the report said.
The file was not closed until 1975 - 15 years after Bevan died.

title: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter
content_c:
Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.
Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports.
The official winter energy forecasts were published days after Europe’s gas market benchmark climbed to its highest level since December 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices rocketing.
National Gas, which runs Great Britain’s gas networks, set out its forecasts after striking an 11th-hour deal with the owner of a major Belgian pipeline to keep gas flowing into the country this winter by reversing a planned capacity cut.
The energy regulator, Ofgem, approved the deal – which will add around 10p a month to the average gas bill. Without the intervention there was a danger of gas running out in the event of a worst-case scenario where an important part of the country’s gas networks failed as temperatures plummeted.
In addition to gas imports by pipelines, Great Britain is expected to increase imports of seaborne liquified natural gas (LNG) cargoes by about 5% from last winter, according to National Gas forecasts, at a time when market prices are three times higher than they were before the Middle East crisis severely disrupted Gulf supplies.
Its winter outlook report suggested that prices could remain elevated if UK gas buyers need to compete more fiercely with countries in Europe for LNG cargoes amid low gas storage levels across the continent.
Europe ended August on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years owing to the slowdown in gas exports from Qatar, one of Europe’s biggest suppliers, and the increase in gas consumption over the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the record heatwaves caused by the global climate crisis.
The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. UK production was forecast to fall by 6% this year compared with last winter, but the government’s controversial decision to approve the new Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea earlier this week, which was not fully accounted for in the winter forecasts, is expected to offer a modest boost to supplies when it starts up next month.
Great Britain is also forecast to be a net importer of electricity over the colder months, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso) separate outlook report. That is also likely to come at a higher cost owing to tighter European power supplies compared with last winter.
The summer heatwaves reduced river levels across Europe, in a blow to French nuclear output and Norway’s hydroelectric reserves, which have remained below the 10-year minimum since late July.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics this week, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid.
Even though Great Britain will use gas power plants less overall this winter compared with previous winters thanks to rising renewable energy levels, the need for gas to play a role during power supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed.
National Gas lifted its gas power demand forecasts for the most extreme electricity supply scenarios – when demand is unusually high and renewable output slumps – after noting over successive winters that gas plants have remained in high use when dark, still winter days lead to high electricity demand and lower renewable energy levels.
Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, said: “While supply diversity and flexibility remain sources of resilience, taken together these trends in demand and supply have resulted in tighter supply margins during periods of high demand and system stress.”

title: Canada's Mark Carney visits Turkey to boost trade ties
content_c:
Canada's Mark Carney visits Turkey to boost trade ties
October 22, 2026
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday to kick off a two-day visit to the Mediterranean country.
During the visit, Carney met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Turkish presidential palace in Ankara.
Erdogan: A 'new era' in Turkey-Canada relations
The two leaders announced that the Canadian-Turkish relationship would be upgraded to a "strategic partnership," covering areas such as trade, energy and people-to-people ties.
"We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both of our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said alongside Erdogan.
Erdogan said we "are starting a new era between Turkey and Canada," while hailing Carney as a leader with "common-sense and acumen." The Turkish leader said negotiations on a free trade agreement with Canada will begin before the end of 2026.
"We hope to increase our trade volume, which is currently around $3 billion (€2.6 billion), to $5 billion and then $10 billion. We will approximately double direct flights between our countries," Erdogan continued.
Canada and Turkey, both members of the NATO military alliance, agreed to deepen their defense relationship during the visit.
Canada seeks to diversify trade relationships amid Trump tariff onslaught
The Canadian prime minister, a former central banker, is expected to meet with Turkish business leaders on Friday in Istanbul.
Carney's visit comes as Canada seeks to broaden its trade relationships with other countries beyond its southern neighbor. Nearly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States.
Since reentering office in 2025, US President Donald Trump escalated a trade war against Canada and imposed tariffs on many Canadian goods, leading Canada to wean itself off the US.
Turkey has a population of over 86 million people and the world's 16th-largest nominal GDP as of 2026. Canada, meanwhile, has a population of over 41 million people and the 11th-largest GDP.
Amnesty tells Canada: Emphasize human rights in negotiations with Turkey
Carney's visit to Turkey also comes as Erdogan and his conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP) crack down on the opposition and critical media. In addition, the Turkish government has targeted the LGBTQ+ community with mass arrests.
Ruhat Sena Aksenir, the Turkey director of human rights watchdog Amnesty International, said: "Canada must not treat human rights as secondary in the negotiations."
"Sustainable partnerships depend on accountability and respect for the rule of law," she continued.
The AKP has ruled Turkey since 2002, with the party, and particularly Erdogan, consolidating power.
According to human rights organization Freedom House, Turkey is "not free" and scores low in the areas of political rights and civil liberties. Reporters without Borders ranks Turkey 163 out of 180 on its World Press Freedom Index.

title: Tunesien: Mann stirbt in U-Haft – Barrikaden brennen in mehreren Städten
content_c:
Ausschreitungen in Nordafrika Mann stirbt in U-Haft – und auf Tunesiens Straßen brennen Barrikaden
Erneut hat es in Tunesien größere Demonstrationen gegeben. Am Donnerstagabend schlugen die Proteste in mehreren Orten in Gewalt um. In dem Vorort Ettadhamen der Hauptstadt Tunis setzten Sicherheitskräfte Tränengas ein, um die Menge auseinanderzutreiben. Zuvor hatten Demonstranten Straßen blockiert, Reifen angezündet und Polizisten mit Steinen beworfen.
Auslöser der Proteste war der Tod eines Mannes, der wegen des Verdachts auf Drogenhandel in Gewahrsam genommen worden war. Nach Angaben seiner Familie starb er infolge von Polizeigewalt. Lokale Medien berichteten dagegen, der Mann habe Drogen verschluckt. Das Innenministerium war für eine Stellungnahme zunächst nicht zu erreichen.
Auch in anderen Teilen des nordafrikanischen Landes kam es zu Unruhen. In der südlichen Stadt Jebeniana stießen Demonstranten mit der Polizei zusammen, nachdem ein Mann nach Angaben von Angehörigen bei einer Verfolgungsjagd mit Sicherheitskräften ums Leben gekommen war.
Ähnliche Ausschreitungen gab es in Agareb. In Sfax protestierten Studenten gegen die unzureichende medizinische Versorgung, nachdem eine Kommilitonin an Herzproblemen gestorben war. Für Freitag riefen sie zu einem Streik an den Universitäten der Stadt auf.
Tausende Menschen zogen durch die Hauptstadt
Die Vorfälle fallen in eine Zeit einer sich verschärfenden wirtschaftlichen, sozialen und politischen Krise in Tunesien. Angesichts der sich verschlechternden Lebensbedingungen und mangelhafter öffentlicher Dienstleistungen wächst die Sorge vor einer landesweiten Protestwelle.

1 Min
Erst am vergangenen Samstag hatten sich in der Hauptstadt an der größten Demonstration gegen Präsident Kais Saied seit Jahren Tausende Menschen beteiligt. Sie werfen ihm vor, die Demokratie zu untergraben und die Wirtschaftskrise des Landes falsch zu handhaben (mehr hier). Die Demonstranten forderten die Freilassung inhaftierter Kritiker des Präsidenten und riefen Parolen wie »Keine Angst, die Macht gehört dem Volk« und »Die Gefängnisse sind voll, die Menschen hungrig«.

title: Korruption - Trumps empfindlichster Punkt vor den Midterms?
content_c:
Vor den Midterms Korruption - Trumps empfindlichster Punkt?
Unter US-Wählern gewinnt vor den Zwischenwahlen ein Thema an Bedeutung - und das ist besonders heikel für Präsident Trump. Immer mehr Bürger registrieren, wie sehr das Vermögen Trumps und seines Umfelds gewachsen ist.
Lisa Gilbert ist eine der prominentesten Stimmen im Kampf gegen politische Korruption in den USA. Die Co-Vorsitzende der Bürgerrechtsorganisation Public Citizen sagt, Geld habe in der US-Politik schon immer eine große Rolle gespielt, Korruption gebe es nicht erst seit Donald Trump. Doch gleichzeitig betont sie: "Unter Trump hat sich das Problem verschärft, ist größer geworden als alles bisher Erlebte."
Zum einen gibt es den Vorwurf, Trump nutze das Präsidentenamt, um für sich und sein privates Umfeld zusätzliches Vermögen anzuhäufen. Zum anderen wird Trump vorgeworfen, er sichere Geldgebern im In- oder Ausland Gegenleistungen, politische Gefälligkeiten zu.
Riesengewinne durch Kryptowährungen
Allein durch Geschäfte mit Krypto-Währungen habe Trump seit Beginn seiner zweiten Amtszeit 1,4 Milliarden Dollar eingenommen, so Gilbert. Wie diese Gewinne zustande kommen, erklärt Mark Hays, Finanzexperte der Bürgerrechtsorganisation Demand Progress, an einem Beispiel: "Eines der großen Geschäfte war der Deal zwischen der Trump-nahen Firma World Liberty Financial und den Vereinigten Arabischen Emiraten."
Die Emirate haben nach seinen Worten zwei Milliarden Dollar in eine von der Trump-nahen Firma in Umlauf gebrachte Kryptowährung investiert. Der Wert der Währung stieg über Nacht sprunghaft an. Und es gab laut Hays eine Gegenleistung: Die Trump-Regierung habe die Export- und Lizenzregeln zugunsten der Emirate gelockert.
Schätzungen im Milliardenbereich
Die Schätzungen, um wie viele Milliarden das Vermögen des Präsidenten und seines privaten Umfelds tatsächlich gewachsen ist, gehen weit auseinander. Demokraten im Kontrollausschuss des Kongresses haben die höchste Summe errechnet: Nehme man Trumps digitale Vermögenswerte, Immobiliengeschäfte und weitere Deals zusammen, ergebe sich seit Beginn seiner zweiten Amtszeit eine Gesamtsumme von 9,7 Milliarden Dollar. Exakt nachweisen lässt sich diese Zahl nicht.
Das Weiße Haus weist alle Vorwürfe zurück und beteuert, der Präsident handle allein im Interesse des Landes. Korruptionsexperten wie Mark Hays sehen das anders. Für sie gibt es eine lange Liste tatsächlicher oder vermuteter Geldflüsse und Gegenleistungen - zum Beispiel, den von Katar geschenkten Jumbo-Jet, den Trump nun als Präsidentenmaschine Air Force One nutzt. Oder Immobiliengeschäfte in mehreren Ländern der Golfregion - von Firmen, die entweder mit Trump selbst, seinem Schwiegersohn Jared Kushner oder seinem langjährigen Vertrauten Steve Witkoff verbunden sind.
Für Mark Hays steht fest: "Der Präsident verschafft nicht nur sich und seinen Freunden finanzielle Vorteile. Er macht Deals auf Kosten nationaler Interessen zugunsten eigener familiärer Interessen."
Geschäft mit Begnadigungen?
Lisa Gilbert, die Co-Vorsitzende der Bürgerrechtsorganisation Public Citizen, nennt weitere Beispiele für fragwürdiges Verhalten Trumps. Der Präsident habe eine Reihe verurteilter Straftäter begnadigt oder deren Strafmaß gemildert, nachdem hohe Summen an politische Organisationskomitees geflossen waren, die Trumps Republikanern nahestehen. "Wir brauchen eine Reform des Begnadigungsrechts", fordert Gilbert. Dabei gilt auch hier: Zusammenhänge gerichtsfest nachzuweisen, bleibt schwierig.
Geld ist aus Sicht von Gilbert auch der Grund, warum Trump die Klimakrise leugnet. Für die Korruptionsexpertin geht es dabei um hohe Summen, die aus der Öl- und Gasindustrie als Wahlkampfspenden an Trump und seine Republikaner fließen: "Das steckt hinter all den schlechten Entscheidungen, die im Bereich Klimawandel getroffen werden."
Deshalb habe Trump die strengeren Abgasnormen für die Autoindustrie zurückgenommen und Subventionen für Windkraft und andere erneuerbare Energien wieder gestrichen. "Als Ölkonzern magst du keine Windräder. Das ist leider der direkte Zusammenhang", so Gilbert.
Lukrative Leugnen des Klimawandels
Einer der Politiker, die sich für schärfere Gesetze in all diesen Bereichen einsetzen, ist der Demokrat Sheldon Whitehouse. Der US-Senator aus dem Bundesstaat Rhode Island spricht von einer "Klimaleugnungs-Betrugsoperation" und einer parallelen "Korruptions-Maschinerie durch Parteispenden".
Allerdings fügt er mit Blick auf die eigene Partei hinzu: Auch die Demokraten hätten bisher viel zu wenig gegen persönliche Bereicherung und Korruption getan. "Wir waren so schwach in der Behandlung dieses Themas, dass die Wähler nicht wissen, ob Demokraten überhaupt besser sind, als Republikaner", so Whitehouse bei einer Konferenz zum Thema Korruptionsbekämpfung in Washington.
Umfragen laufen gegen Trump
Kurz vor den Kongress-Zwischenwahlen scheint sich die Stimmung allerdings immer mehr gegen Präsident Trump und seine Republikaner zur wenden. Die Nachrichtenagentur AP hat eine Umfrage veröffentlicht, nach der 59 Prozent der Amerikanerinnen und Amerikaner der Ansicht sind, dass Trump mehr am eigenen Profit interessiert ist als am Wohl der Bürger.
41 Prozent der repräsentativ Befragten stufen das Verhalten ihres Präsidenten als illegal ein, weitere 18 Prozent als zumindest unethisch. Nach einer Umfrage des Fernsehsenders Fox News ist Korruption in der Liste der Themen, die Wählerinnen und Wählern Sorgen machen, ganz nach vorn an Nummer eins gerückt - noch vor die Themen Inflation und Benzinpreise.

title: РФ знайшла нові цілі для ударів в Києві і змінює тактику атак: аналітики попередили про небезпеку для цивільних
content_c:
РФ знайшла нові цілі для ударів в Києві і змінює тактику атак: аналітики попередили про небезпеку для цивільних
Касетні боєприпаси належать до категорії зброї невибіркової дії, головною метою якої є завдання максимальних страждань цивільним людям і забруднення української землі, зазначають експерти.
Росія застосувала касетні балістичні ракети для удару по історичному центру Києва. Це є новим небезпечним етапом ескалації повітряного терору.
Про це йдеться у звіті аналітиків Інституту вивчення війни (ISW).
«Російські війська завдали удару по Києву касетними боєприпасами, щоб навмисно завдати шкоди цивільному населенню, ймовірно, в рамках ширших російських зусиль, спрямованих на відволікання уваги від нещодавніх успіхів України на полі бою та зрештою змусити Україну до капітуляції, зробивши повсякденне життя нестерпним», — йдеться у повідомленні аналітиків.
Експерти наголошують, що касетні боєприпаси мають широку зону ураження і призначені для знищення живої сили противника або легкої технікию
«Це підкреслює намір Росії завдати максимальної шкоди та страждань цивільному населенню», — додали аналітики.
Нагадаємо, Росія вночі, 22 жовтня, навмисно обстріляла центр Києва балістичними ракетами з касетними боєголовками. Внаслідок атаки було пошкоджено історичний центр столиці в районі між Києво-Печерською лаврою та Свято-Введенським монастирем.
Президент України Володимир Зеленський повідомив, що РФ застосувала три балістичні ракети з касетними боєголовками.
«Ці ракети розроблені таким чином, щоб детонувати в повітрі під час наближення до цілей, поширюючи пошкодження на площі діаметром 400 метрів», — пояснив він.

title: Спутники сделали снимок антарктического «слона», покрытого снегом
content_c:
Спутники миссии Copernicus Sentinel-3 Европейского космического агентства (ESA) сделали детальные снимки Западной Антарктики. На них попал остров Мордвинова, известный также как Элефант (от английского Elephant Island или остров Слон), сообщает Space.com.
В Южном полушарии заканчивается зима. Это период, когда ледовые условия достигают своего пика, а площадь морского льда становится максимальной.
На снимке, который сделал спутник Sentinel-3, виден обширный ледяной массив, в который входит остров Элефант, расположенный в левой части изображения. Этот покрытый льдом остров находится у побережья Антарктиды, в водах Южного океана. Свое название он получил из-за формы, которая некоторым людям напоминает голову слона. Кроме того на острове обитает популяция морских слонов.
На снимке можно также увидеть ландшафт Антарктиды протяженностью примерно от 1200 до 1700 километров. Изображение получили 30 сентября. В Южном полушарии это время пришлось на период сразу после окончания зимы. По данным Национального центра данных по снегу и льду США, на которые ссылается ESA, пик площади морского льда в Антарктиде был зафиксирован всего за пару недель до этого — 14 сентября. То есть, на изображении можно увидеть состояние морского льда Антарктики, близкое к максимуму.
Напомним, в 2024 году в морском льду Антарктики появилась гигантская дыра или «полынья». До этого ученые не наблюдали ничего подобного зимой. На пике своего развития площадь этой полыньи достигала 89 121 квадратного километра, что немного меньше площади Португалии.
description: Остров Мордвинова омывается Южным океаном.
content:
Спутники миссии Copernicus Sentinel-3 Европейского космического агентства (ESA) сделали детальные снимки Западной Антарктики. На них попал остров Мордвинова, известный также как Элефант (от английского Elephant Island или остров Слон), сообщает Space.com.
В Южном полушарии заканчивается зима. Это период, когда ледовые условия достигают своего пика, а площадь морского льда становится максимальной.
На снимке, который сделал спутник Sentinel-3, виден обширный ледяной массив, в который входит остров Элефант, расположенный в левой части изображения. Этот покрытый льдом остров находится у побережья Антарктиды, в водах Южного океана. Свое название он получил из-за формы, которая некоторым людям напоминает голову слона. Кроме того на острове обитает популяция морских слонов.
На снимке можно также увидеть ландшафт Антарктиды протяженностью примерно от 1200 до 1700 километров. Изображение получили 30 сентября. В Южном полушарии это время пришлось на период сразу после окончания зимы. По данным Национального центра данных по снегу и льду США, на которые ссылается ESA, пик площади морского льда в Антарктиде был зафиксирован всего за пару недель до этого — 14 сентября. То есть, на изображении можно увидеть состояние морского льда Антарктики, близкое к максимуму.
Напомним, в 2024 году в морском льду Антарктики появилась гигантская дыра или «полынья». До этого ученые не наблюдали ничего подобного зимой. На пике своего развития площадь этой полыньи достигала 89 121 квадратного километра, что немного меньше площади Португалии.

title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
content_c:
Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
- Published
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.
In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.
In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.
It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.
A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.
It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".
"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.
Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.
Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.
Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.
Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.
On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network".
The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.
Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power".
He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes.
Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

title: Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
content_c:
Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
- Published
Andy Burnham's decision to appoint John Healey to the crucial role of chancellor of the exchequer was the rarest of things at Westminster - a genuine surprise.
It's not that the 66-year-old lacked experience or credibility - just that he had not been seen as a likely contender, with all the speculation about who would replace Rachel Reeves centring on more high-profile figures.
Healey had flown under the radar since his explosive resignation as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June this year.
His assessment of the government's defence investment plan - that it fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time" - was devastating and undoubtedly hastened Sir Keir's departure from Downing Street.
But his resignation letter also included pointed criticism of Reeves's Treasury, which he said had been "unwilling" to "commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats".
Now he is in the Treasury hot seat and under pressure to spell out how he will get defence spending up to 3% of national income, at the same time as cutting government borrowing costs and tackling the cost of living.
Like his predecessor, he faces the difficult balancing act of keeping Labour MPs happy without spooking the financial markets, while delivering on the government's key priorities.
Never the flashiest of politicians, his early speeches as chancellor have been focused on stressing his commitment to fiscal discipline and cutting the welfare bill, as well as banging the drum for Burnham's plan to "reindustrialise" Britain.
But he did show his lighter side in a social media video with the prime minister, which saw "Andy and John" bantering about twiglets and scampi fries in the pub., external
"I will always stand by my political choices as chancellor, including pork scratchings as the best pub snack," he revealed on X.
John Healey: The Basics
Age: 66
Place of birth: Wakefield, West Yorkshire
Education: Lady Lumley's Academy, Pickering; St Peter's School, York; Christ's College, Cambridge
Family: He married Jackie Bate in 1993. The couple have one son, Alex
Constituency: MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, in South Yorkshire
Salary: £166,000
- What is the Budget and what could be in it? 
  - Published2 days ago
- Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor 
  - Published28 September
The softly-spoken Yorkshireman has a remarkable record as someone who has been on the Labour frontbench almost continuously since 2001.
Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge.
Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official.
He is married and has one son.
He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough.
He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place.
In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments.
He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government.
Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson, Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government."
He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future".
And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans.
"The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson.
Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016.
When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later.
Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky.
At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face".
Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families, with a £9bn spending plan.
Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies.
In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you.
"We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences."
Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get.
Healey also made clear that he wanted a clear plan to increase UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
He is not expected to do that in his first Budget, with key spending decisions set to be unveiled next year.
But the tax and spending decisions he does announce on 28 October will still have a huge impact on the success or failure of the fledgling Burnham administration.

title: Milan braces for more unrest as debate intensifies over Italy’s ‘lost generation’
content_c:
Martina Miccichè was filming riot police kicking and beating a teenager with batons as they dragged him along Piazza del Duomo, the central Milan square hosting its cathedral, when she was struck by a flying object, causing a deep gash and bruising near her right eye.
The journalist had joined hundreds of mostly young people marching through the northern Italian city on Saturday afternoon to protest over soaring living costs and unaffordable housing, echoing the wider wave of economic discontent fuelling protests across Europe.
It wasn’t the first time Italy’s youth have loudly aired their grievances during Giorgia Meloni’s four years as prime minister, despite the risk of falling foul of her ruling coalition’s ever-expanding crackdown on security and public dissent. On Saturday afternoon they plan to protest again in Milan and other major Italian cities.
Miccichè said the atmosphere last Saturday was peaceful until about 5pm, when police blocked access to Via Broletto, a street about a 10-minute walk away from Piazza del Duomo.
“People were angry because they were being repressed,” she said, claiming the police turned “suddenly violent” as they pushed the crowd back with their shields. “The violence escalated. They started to grab people at random, hitting and kicking them. It was shocking.”
As the clashes continued and police filled the square with teargas while astonished tourists looked on, a group of masked youths on the fringes headed to the surrounding fashion district, tearing down road signs, setting bins alight and smashing shop windows – among them Footlocker and Levi’s – then looting them.
The vandalism resumed on Sunday as the gangs – many baited by the promise of luxury goods through a network of social media chats – descended on the city centre again, mostly from marginalised areas on the outskirts.
During the two days of unrest, police detained more than 271 young people. Of those, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals.
As the Italian media published images of injured police officers, Meloni’s government rapidly enacted more measures targeting minors and further empowering the police – including holding parents financially accountable for their children’s vandalism and looting – while dispatching 500 troops to Milan.
The latest legislation also criminalises violent participation in a demonstration and toughens penalties for rioters.
Some of the government’s security measures are now being applied in the south of Italy, where lorry drivers have been protesting against high petrol prices for more than a week, blocking roads and disrupting supermarket supplies. In response, 71 people have been reported to judicial authorities and 242 fined over the blockades – a protest act made illegal in a previous security bill. A government official also warned the lorry drivers that obstructing public highways could carry jail terms.
“This government just tries to repress protesters instead of listening to them and addressing the issues,” said Miccichè, who needed stitches for her injury. “It is all connected. There is anger in the south over fuel prices and young people everywhere are angry – they don’t even have a chance to think about the future because they are so terrified of the present.”
Furthermore, “we are not feeling safe”, the 34-year-old added, “because we can see how much space the police have now and how shielded they are”. Racial profiling had become the norm in Milan, especially in the centre and close to its train stations, she claimed.
The weekend’s urban unrest, including protests in Turin and Bologna, has intensified debate over Italy’s “lost generation”.
Furthermore, the youth protests and subsequent fringe violence have exposed the sharp divide between Italy’s marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects.
Working-class Italians or third- and second-generation immigrants are regularly labelled by rightwing politicians and the press as maranza, a derogatory term used to describe groups of young people who usually congregate in city centres.
They come from areas like Barona, a sprawling council estate in the south-west of Milan. Young people there have been reflecting on the events of last weekend. “There is a lot of discontent – we are all children of this widespread malaise,” said Domenico Ricci, who along with Luca Orlando manages a bar that is part of Barrio’s, a cultural hub where the district’s youth come together.
Orlando believes the vandalism and looting were a symptom of anger and years of feeling unheard and invisible. “So when an opportunity arises, these kids take revenge. They don’t do it simply because they want to steal something. All this government does is introduce new crimes – they never listen or engage in dialogue.”
Orlando, whose parents came from Calabria, is feeling the nationwide discontent. “But the protests there [in the south-west] have hardly had any coverage,” he said. “And we are only talking about Milan because of the violence and not the real issues.”
Thomas, 18, who has grown up in Barona, is training to be a chef and wants to leave Italy “as soon as possible”. He said: “I see no future here.” His friend Mohamed, an Italian citizen of Moroccan origin, is still at high school and wants to become a lawyer. “If you make a mistake, then you must pay,” he said. “But this is also a characteristic of protests – the more a government doesn’t listen, the more people get angry.”
Mauro Magatti, a sociologist at Milan’s Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, said socioeconomic discomfort and a sense of abandonment affected “an entire generation” and responding to the anger with excessive repression risked enlarging the protest. “Violence always needs to be condemned but now we need to lower the tone to overcome this burst of anger and violence and focus on addressing the real problems,” he said.
Police and military presence in central Milan has been building in recent days before Saturday’s protest, organised by a new online movement which has pledged to gather each weekend “until this government of thieves falls”. Security guards stood outside shops that had been damaged or looted last weekend.
Italy’s politicians from across the spectrum must take heed, warned Miccichè, as the protests were only set to amplify ahead of general elections next year. “There is no perception at all of how young people feel,” she said. “Even if they took just a minute to listen, they will understand that it is a generation full of ideas – they just want to be heard.”

French President Macron bans 'illegitimate' protests in coming days
October 22, 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that demonstrations organized by groups without legitimate authority would be banned in the coming days.
Over the past weekend, protests over the education system and the cost of living escalated into violence and looting, which the government blamed on ultra-left groups.
"Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron said after a special security meeting at the Elysee Palace with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers.
"The general recommendation is not to hold demonstrations in the coming days," he explained. "We want calm to return."
Macron said the ban on protests aimed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed," he added.
Fresh demonstration in Paris
In the wake of the past weekend’s violence, several cities had already implemented curfews for certain parts of town. Protests planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned from going ahead.
Authorities say a massive security operation was planned for the coming weekend to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence.
Student and university groups as well as unions have said they would continue to mobilize and hold protests. On Thursday, thousands gathered in Paris when a local court was said to have overturned the day's demonstration ban.
France's main student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook the country in 2018 and 2019, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.
What are the protests about?
The protests started in September at a school near Paris over lack of funding for the education system.
The demonstrations then spread to other Paris suburbs and eventually to other French cities. They have since widened to also address the soaring cost of living and deteriorating public services.
On October 17, the protests escalated into the worst urban unrest in years when masked rioters clashed with police, looted shops and set cars and buildings on fire.
Two people have been arrested over an arson attack on the 19th-century Limoges city hall, French media reported.
Across France, there were around 2,700 arrests last weekend and hundreds of protesters, police and firefighters were injured.
French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said courts jailed 217 people in fast-track trials linked to rioting over the weekend, adding "this figure is continuing to rise a lot."
Macron on Thursday said talks between authorities, student groups, unions, and employers would take place on Monday. He stressed that dialogue over protesters' legitimate demands should continue.
The unrest comes just months before next year's presidential election, in which voters will choose Macron's successor.

title: Erstes Atommüllendlager weltweit erhält Betriebsgenehmigung
content_c:
Errichtet in finnischem Felsgestein Erstes Atommüllendlager weltweit erhält Betriebsgenehmigung
Finnland hat den Betrieb des weltweit ersten Endlagers für abgebrannte Kernbrennstoffe genehmigt. Wie das Entsorgungsunternehmen Posiva am Donnerstag erklärte, soll das Lager in der Gemeinde Eurajoki im Südwesten Finnlands bald den Betrieb aufnehmen, ein genaues Datum steht demnach aber noch nicht fest.
Der Bau des unterirdischen Lagers namens »Onkalo«, Finnisch für Höhle, war vor 22 Jahren begonnen worden. (Lesen Sie hier eine Reportage vom Bau der Anlage .) Atomkraftwerke werden deutlich schneller errichtet: Je nach Land und Reaktortyp dauert es meist zwischen 7 und 15 Jahren.
Posiva-Geschäftsführer Ilkka Poikolainen sprach von einem »großartigen und historischen Tag sowohl für Posiva als auch für Finnland«. Bevor mit der Endlagerung begonnen wird, werde Posiva die erforderlichen Tests und Inspektionen durchführen, die auch von der finnischen Behörde für Strahlenschutz und nukleare Sicherheit überprüft und genehmigt werden müssen, erklärte das Unternehmen.
Bauarbeiten im Fels im Mai 2023
Foto: Jonathan Nackstrand / AFP
Das Endlager ist in ein 1,9 Milliarden Jahre altes, festes Grundgestein gebohrt worden und bietet Kapazität für 6500 Tonnen Uran. Es soll als Lager für abgebrannte Brennelemente aus den fünf finnischen Kernreaktoren dienen, die noch jahrtausendelang hoch radioaktiv sein werden.
Die Brennelemente sollen in korrosionsbeständige Kupferbehälter eingekapselt und dann in Bohrlöcher in den Tunneln im Felsgestein abgesenkt werden, die wiederum gefüllt und mit einem stahlverstärkten Betonstopfen verschlossen werden sollen.
-

- 
2 Min
- 
Hoch radioaktive Abfälle: 25 Prozent der Fläche Deutschlands kommen für Atommüllendlager infrage2 Min2 Min
Seit dem Bau der ersten Kernkraftwerke in den Fünfzigerjahren ringen Länder mit der Frage, wie mit gefährlichem Atommüll umgegangen werden soll. Derzeit wird der größte Teil davon zwischengelagert.
Auch in anderen Ländern, darunter Schweden und Frankreich, werden Endlagerstätten gebaut. Finnland wird jedoch voraussichtlich das erste Land sein, das sein unterirdisches Lager in Betrieb nimmt.

title: Energiepreise: Ministerpräsidenten drängen auf Entlastungen
content_c:
Stromsteuer und Spritpreise Ministerpräsidentenkonferenz drängt auf schnelle Entlastungen
Die Stromsteuer runter, die Kraftstoffkosten deckeln: Die Ministerpräsidentinnen und -präsidenten fordern von der Regierung spürbare Entlastungen für die Menschen im Land. Man sei der Auffassung, dass der Bund diese Spielräume habe.
Die Energiepreise sind in den vergangenen Monaten infolge internationaler Krisen stark gestiegen. Geht es nach den Bundesländern, sollten Verbraucher in Deutschland deshalb möglichst rasch von den Kosten entlastet werden.
In einem Beschluss mahnte die Ministerpräsidentenkonferenz (MPK) in Berlin die Bundesregierung zu einer schnellen Senkung der Stromsteuer für alle an. Dazu forderte die MPK einen zeitnahen Vorschlag für einen Spritpreisdeckel.
In dem Beschluss zur Stromsteuer heißt es, die Energiepreise seien trotz aller Entlastungsmaßnahmen im internationalen Vergleich weiterhin zu hoch. "Die Regierungschefinnen und Regierungschefs der Länder fordern die Bundesregierung daher auf, schnellstmöglich finanzielle Spielräume im Haushalt für eine Senkung der Stromsteuer für alle zu nutzen", hieß es.
Stromsteuer bereits im Koalitionsvertrag
Man sei der Auffassung, dass der Bund diese Spielräume habe, erklärte der MPK-Vorsitzende, der rheinland-pfälzische Ministerpräsident Gordon Schnieder (CDU). "Wir haben den Menschen versprochen, dass Energie bezahlbarer wird, insbesondere dass Strom für alle günstiger wird. Dieses Versprechen müssen wir halten."
Die Senkung der Stromsteuer war bereits im Koalitionsvertrag von Schwarz-Rot vorgesehen. Bislang wurde sie jedoch nur für Industrie, Forst- und Landwirtschaft umgesetzt. Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) plädierte zuletzt zwar für eine Senkung für alle. Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) sieht dafür jedoch im Haushalt bislang keine Spielräume.
"Tankrabatt" gilt nur begrenzt
Auch zur langfristigen Begrenzung der Kraftstoffpreise soll die Bundesregierung nach dem Willen der Ministerpräsidenten möglichst bald einen Vorschlag machen. Man wolle einen Spritpreisdeckel nutzen, um den Menschen die Sicherheit zu geben, "dass es eine Form von Gerechtigkeit gibt, dass sie nicht an der Tankstelle für Unternehmen zahlen, die damit ihre Gewinne erhöhen", sagte Niedersachsens Regierungschef Olaf Lies (SPD).
Die Bundesregierung hatte zuletzt in Aussicht gestellt, mit der Mineralölwirtschaft über einen Spritpreisdeckel zu sprechen. Ziel sei, den Deckel bis spätestens zum 1. Januar einzuführen. Derzeit gilt in Deutschland ein "Tankrabatt" von 16,7 Cent pro Liter. Die Maßnahme ist allerdings befristet bis Jahresende. Sie kommt einer Untersuchung des Ifo-Instituts zufolge dazu nach wie vor nicht vollständig bei den Autofahrern an.
Seit Beginn des Iran-Kriegs Ende Februar waren die Energiepreise international drastisch gestiegen, insbesondere durch eingeschränkte Öl- und Gaslieferungen durch die Straße von Hormus. Die wichtige Seestraße ist seit Beginn des Kriegs für den Welthandel weitgehend blockiert. Immer wieder kommt es auch zu Angriffen auf Tanker, die versuchen, die Meerenge zu passieren.
