title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
content_c:
'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
- Published
Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable".
Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done".
In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.
The ad set off a storm of criticism from members of both parties. On Thursday, President Donald Trump sought to defend it and Ramaswamy on social media.
And at a rally in Iowa late on Thursday, Trump advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it".
"Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much'," he added.
Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.
In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.
"I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening.
"You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad.
The last time Acton saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted, according to Acton's campaign.
Arthur's husband fled the state before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004. Arthur left with him.
In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".
Trump, who has endorsed Ramaswamy, blamed the press for the negative reaction to the ad, in a long post where he also commended Arthur and Ramaswamy. Trump blasted DeWine, as well.
He urged Ramaswamy to keep up his attacks and "let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!"
"I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse," Trump also posted.
In the ad, Arthur repeatedly says Acton lies and asserts she "needs help", but does not discuss anything related to cheating or stealing.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.
Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.
The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".
On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor.
"And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."
MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.
Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.
David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense".
He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour.
A poll by VoteHub, external released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad.
If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades.

title: Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn
content_c:
Heat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, new research suggests, with scientists blaming climate breakdown for two in every three of the deaths.
Morgues and funeral homes filled with bodies from June to August as the heat added by planet-baking pollution cut short an extra 32,000 lives in urban areas, the researchers found. Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.
The “staggering” death toll, modelled using historical relationships between heat and health in 854 cities, was the worst on record, the study found. Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years.
“In some sense, the absolute numbers of the heat-related deaths estimated across the 854 urban areas are indeed staggering,” said Malcolm Mistry, a climate and health scientist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who co-authored the study. “But perhaps what is even more alarming is the proportion of these deaths that we attribute to anthropogenic climate change.”
The share of deaths due to climate breakdown has risen from about 40% at the start of the century to 65% this summer, the study found.
People succumbed to heat at the highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, while absolute death tolls were greatest in Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Because death certificates rarely record contributing factors – such as dangerous temperatures that push a stroke victim or lung cancer patient past their limits – families rarely know that heat and human activity hastened their relatives’ death.
“These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost a loved one this summer due to the climate crisis,” said Katie White, the climate transition minister for the UK, where scientists estimated 4,354 heat deaths this summer.”
In Naples, the hardest-hit city on the continent, 815 people per million died from the heat, according to the study’s age-standardised estimates. Mario Guarino, an emergency doctor at Ospedale CTO in the north of the city, said he witnessed a 15% increase in emergency room visits during the hottest weeks.
The “defining characteristic” of the period was the complexity of health problems exacerbated by heat, he added, with loneliness and poverty worsening the situation further.
“We took in a terminal cancer patient who lived in a hot attic simply because his family couldn’t find a company to install air conditioning during the summer,” said Guarino. “An elderly man with dementia was abruptly abandoned by his Ukrainian caregiver who returned home to say goodbye to her son, who had been called to war. Emergency services found [the man] lying on the floor one night with a fractured pelvis, desperately trying to call the tenant next door.”
The study found people over the age of 85 made up almost half of the death toll, though younger people were not immune, with 833 people between the age of 20 and 44 also thought to have died due to the heat. The scientists said the death toll from the cities studied, which account for about 40% of the European population, could not be easily extrapolated to estimate the full death toll including those in towns and villages.
The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, the EU’s climate monitoring service announced this month, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Slightly less punishing temperatures in eastern Europe brought the continental average to its third-hottest level on record.
Greenhouse gases have warmed Europe about twice as fast as the global average, exposing more people to intolerably hot summers and fewer people to dangerously cold winters. While cold is a bigger killer than heat, scientists expect rising temperatures to claim more lives than they save, as heat deaths are projected to rise faster than cold deaths fall.
The study combined established relationships between heat and mortality with temperature data for 2026 to rapidly estimate the fallout from this summer’s heat. The death tolls for individual countries differ from what national public health agencies have calculated using their own methods.
David García-García, a researcher at the mortality monitoring system at the Carlos III health institute in Madrid, who was not involved in the study, said it was a “valuable contribution” that allowed for comparisons across the continent. “However, it is important to bear in mind that these are estimates based on observed temperatures and epidemiological models, which do not incorporate actual data on deaths occurring in the summer of 2026,” he said.
Doctors have urged governments to burn fewer fossil fuels – the core driver of rising temperatures – while bolstering health systems, greening cities, rolling out air conditioning and encouraging people to drink water and seek shade. They have also stressed the benefits of people checking in on vulnerable neighbours and family members so they can get help before tragedy strikes.
“The real epidemic these days is loneliness,” said Guarino. “Many elderly people are left alone during the summer, abandoned by their families, and due to their low income, they can’t afford air conditioning or, if they do have it, avoid turning it on because of the cost of electricity.”

title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
content_c:
Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
October 22, 2026
Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes
following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.
The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.
Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump's Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September.
After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.
Report: Plans in place for 'short' US-Israeli operation
Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country's arsenal of missiles and drones.
One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.
Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."
There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.
On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.
A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.
Has Iran learned from earlier attacks?
Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.
Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country rather than matching US strength.
"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.
Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.
Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.
Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
How Iran prepares for new strikes?
Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.
Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."
Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.
Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.
Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.
Fear of war inside Iran
An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.
A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."
Edited: Emmy Sasipornkarn

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
How Iran prepares for new strikes?
Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.
Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."
Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.
Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.
Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.
Fear of war inside Iran
An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.
A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."

title: Tote und Verletzte bei starkem Erdbeben in China
content_c:
Magnitude 7,0 Tote und Verletzte bei starkem Erdbeben in China
Bei dem schweren Erdbeben in China sind mindestens 16 Menschen ums Leben gekommen. Mindestens 32 weitere seien bei dem Unglück in der Autonomen Region Tibet verletzt worden, berichtete die staatliche chinesische Nachrichtenagentur Xinhua unter Berufung auf den Katastrophenschutz der Stadt Nagqu. Elf der Verletzten befanden sich demnach in kritischem Zustand. Durch die Erschütterungen seien mehr als 300 Häuser eingestürzt, berichtete Xinhua weiter.
Das Erdbeben der Stärke 7,0 ereignete sich nach Angaben des US-Geologischen Dienstes (USGS) und der chinesischen Erdbeben-Beobachtungsstelle (CENC) um 16.33 Uhr MESZ (22.33 Uhr Ortszeit) rund 180 Kilometer nordöstlich von Nagqu in einer Tiefe von zehn Kilometern. Seitdem wurden in der Region mehrere Nachbeben registriert.
Laut USGS leben etwa 100.000 Menschen so nah am Epizentrum, dass das Beben für sie deutlich wahrnehmbar war. Der Geologische Dienst hat aus den Daten des Bebens und der Beschaffenheit der Häuser eine Prognose für die Zahl getöteter Menschen berechnet. Die Wahrscheinlichkeit für mehr als 100 Todesopfer liegt demnach bei 16 Prozent, am wahrscheinlichsten seien 10 bis 100 Tote.
Das Beben war im Kreis Baqing aufgetreten, der zur Stadt Nagqu gehört. Tibets Hauptstadt Lhasa liegt etwa 400 Kilometer weiter südwestlich. Die Gegend um Nagqu gilt als dünn besiedelt. Das Gebiet im Bereich des Epizentrums liegt laut Xinhua durchschnittlich auf einer Höhe von 4800 Metern. Mit einer Stärke von 7,0 war dieses Erdbeben das bisher stärkste in diesem Jahr in China.
Der stellvertretende Gemeindevorsteher Lhawang Dagpo berichtete laut Xinhua, die Erschütterungen seien im Verwaltungsgebäude deutlich zu spüren gewesen und hätten Risse in den Wänden verursacht. Im Hauptort des Kreises waren demnach die Stromversorgung und die Telekommunikation beeinträchtigt. Die Behörden aktivierten laut Xinhua die zweithöchste Katastrophenschutzstufe.

title: Marktbericht: DAX fällt wieder zurück
content_c:
Tech-Aktien im Fokus DAX fällt wieder zurück
Der DAX hat bei volatilem Handel einen Teil seiner Gewinne vom Vortag wieder abgegeben. Er folgte einer schwachen Wall Street. Es waren mal wieder Nachrichten aus dem US-Tech-Sektor, die die Kurse bewegten.
Zur Wochenmitte war es noch ein überraschend starkes Ergebnis von Elon Musks Weltraum- und KI-Konglomerat SpaceX, das die Stimmung der Anleger aufhellte. Heute kam nun die Ernüchterung. Denn die am Vortag nach Börsenschluss in New York veröffentlichten Ergebnisse der drei Tech-Größen Meta, IBM und Tesla wurden negativ aufgenommen.
Da half es auch nur bedingt, dass DAX-Schwergewicht SAP überzeugte, sich im Handelsverlauf von Anfangsverlusten erholte und im Plus schloss. Das Mega-Thema Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) bestimmt immer wieder entscheidend das Geschehen und sorgt weltweit für volatile Märkte - auch wenn die Hauptprotagonisten fast allesamt in den USA sitzen.
Der DAX gab bei wechselhaftem Handel einen Teil seiner gestrigen Gewinne wieder ab und konnte sich letztlich nur leicht von seinen Tiefständen lösen. Am Ende schloss der deutsche Leitindex bei 25.371 Punkten um 1,1 Prozent leichter. Am Vortag hatte der Index noch gut 1,3 Prozent zugelegt. Das Tagestief lag am Vormittag bei 25.318 Punkten.
Die Furcht der Anleger vor Lieferausfällen wegen einer Eskalation des Konflikts im Nahen Osten treibt derweil die Ölpreise erneut in die Höhe. Ein Fass (159 Liter) der Nordseesorte Brent verteuert sich um etwa 2,6 Prozent auf gut 112 Dollar. Auslöser waren erneute Angriffe der vom Iran unterstützten Huthi-Miliz auf Ziele in Saudi-Arabien.
Die US-Regierung wies daraufhin Diplomaten und deren Familien an, ihre Vertretungen in Saudi-Arabien zu verlassen. Zudem berichtete die Zeitung New York Times, die Streitkräfte der USA und Israels hätten Pläne für erneute Angriffe auf Iran nach den US-Zwischenwahlen am 3. November ausgearbeitet.
"Die Bemühungen, die Spannungen sowohl in der Ukraine als auch im Nahen Osten zu entschärfen, sind nicht überzeugend", kommentierte Tamas Varga, Ölexperte beim Makler PVM.
Sorgen bereitet den Anlegern auch weiterhin die Lage in Frankreich. Sie warfen heute erneut französische Staatsanleihen aus ihren Depots. Die Rendite zehnjähriger französischer Staatsanleihen stieg in der Spitze auf rund 5,11 Prozent und lag damit erstmals seit 2013 über der von vergleichbaren US-Staatsanleihen.
Gründe für die wachsende Nervosität sind die hohe Verschuldung Frankreichs, die politische Unsicherheit vor der Präsidentschaftswahl im kommenden Jahr und Schwierigkeiten bei der Verabschiedung des Haushalts. Anhaltende Straßenproteste belasten die Stimmung zusätzlich. Im Gegenzug legten die Kurse der Bundesanleihen zu - deren Rendite fiel dadurch auf zuletzt 3,34 Prozent.
Vor allem an der Technologiebörse Nasdaq geht es in New York kräftig bergab. Während der Dow Jones-Index, der Leitindex der Standardwerte, am Mittag Ortszeit kaum verändert tendiert, verliert der Auswahlindex Nasdaq 100 rund zwei Prozent. Neben deutlich gestiegenen Ölpreisen verderben die negativ aufgenommene Ergebnisse von Branchengrößen wie Meta, Tesla oder IBM zur Geschäftsentwicklung den Anlegern die Stimmung.
"Die Botschaft scheint immer deutlicher zu werden: Der Markt ist nach wie vor bereit, hohe Investitionen in KI zu belohnen, stellt jedoch immer höhere Anforderungen an die Renditen", sagte Santiago Mateo, Leiter des Aktienbereichs bei CaixaBank AM. "Die Anleger wollen Nachweise dafür, dass sich die Investitionen in ein stärkeres Wachstum, eine bessere Monetarisierung und letztendlich in Gewinnen niederschlagen."
Genau hier wächst die Skepsis und Ungeduld der Anleger. Bestes Beispiel ist Meta. Der Internetkonzern investiert im laufenden Jahr mit 135 bis 145 Milliarden Dollar gigantische Summen in den Ausbau seiner KI-Infrastruktur. Das Geld dafür liefert weiter das boomende Werbegeschäft.
Der Gewinn wird allerdings durch Kosten für Rechtsstreitigkeiten schwer belastet. Fast zehn Milliarden Dollar muss Konzernchef Mark Zuckerberg dafür zurückstellen. Hinzu kommt noch, dass wenige Stunden vor Veröffentlichung der Zwischenbilanz ein Richter das Unternehmen zu einer Strafe von 25 Milliarden Dollar verurteilte.
Auch Tesla muss hohe Kosten für KI-Investitionen stemmen. Elon Musk möchte Tesla auf selbstfahrende Robotaxis und humanoide Roboter ausrichten. Deshalb wird es Musk nicht gefallen, dass der Gewinn um mehr als 40 Prozent eingebrochen ist. Nur rund 800 Millionen Dollar blieben unter dem Strich hängen, der Umsatz stagnierte bei rund 28,05 Milliarden Dollar.

title: РФ розбила одну з теплоелектростанцій: об’єкт зупинив роботу
content_c:
РФ розбила одну з теплоелектростанцій: об’єкт зупинив роботу
Після російської атаки станція зупинила генерацію електроенергії.
Російська армія атакувала одну з теплоелектростанцій ДТЕК. Внаслідок обстрілу станція припинила генерацію електроенергії.
Про це повідомили у пресслужбі холдингу.
«Росія масовано обстріляла одну з ТЕС ДТЕК», — наголосили в компанії.
Зазначається, що було суттєво пошкоджено обладнання ТЕС. Наразі оцінюють масштаби руйнувань.
Водночас у ДТЕК додали, що від початку повномасштабного вторгнення ТЕС були атаковані понад 230 разів.
Ситуація в енергетиці — що відомо
Останні часом РФ посилила атаки на енергетичну інфраструктуру в різних регіонах України. Днями президент Володимир Зеленський заявив, що під час останніх хвиль ударів було уражено майже 30 підстанцій та інші об’єкти енергетики.
Енергетичний експерт Юрій Корольчук наголошує, що цієї зими в Україні можуть посилити відключення електроенергії через пошкодження енергетичної інфраструктури. За несприятливого розвитку подій у деяких регіонах світла може не бути понад 20 годин на добу.
Тим часом експерт енергетичних програм Центру Разумкова Володимир Омельченко попереджає про загрозу для Києва. Столиця може зіткнутися не лише з тривалими відключеннями світла, а ще й з перебоями з водопостачанням і проблемами з теплом в окремих районах.

title: Инцидент с украинским «Русланом» в Японии: что известно
content_c:
В Японии во время посадки крупного грузового самолета Ан-124 «Руслан» украинской авиакомпании Antonov Airlines с борта было замечено пламя. Из-за инцидента в аэропорту Chubu Centrair недалеко от Нагои временно закрыли взлетно-посадочную полосу.
Инцидент произошел вечером 22 октября в международном аэропорту Chubu Centrair в городе Токонаме, префектура Айти.
Как сообщает японский NewsDigest со ссылкой на пресс-службу Министерства земли, инфраструктуры, транспорта и туризма Японии, в аэропорту Тюбу во время посадки крупного грузового самолета с его борта было видно пламя.
На опубликованных очевидцами кадрах также видна вспышка пламени в задней части самолета.
По состоянию на 20:10 по местному времени специалисты ещё не установили причину возникновения пожара. Взлётно-посадочную полосу после инцидента временно закрыли, однако, по информации японских властей, это не оказало существенного влияния на движение пассажирских рейсов.
По данным сервиса отслеживания полётов Plane Finder, 22 октября в Нагою прибыл Ан-124-100 украинской авиакомпании Antonov Airlines с бортовым номером UR-82029.
Самолет выполнял грузовой рейс ADB5561 из Фербанкса на Аляске в Нагою. Plane Finder идентифицирует его как Antonov An-124-100 и указывает в качестве оператора Antonov Airlines.
В соцсетях пользователи предполагают, что источником пламени мог быть двигатель или вспомогательная силовая установка самолета. Официально причина инцидента остается неизвестной.

Как сообщает японский NewsDigest со ссылкой на пресс-службу Министерства земли, инфраструктуры, транспорта и туризма Японии, в аэропорту Тюбу во время посадки крупного грузового самолета с его борта было видно пламя.
На опубликованных очевидцами кадрах также видна вспышка пламени в задней части самолета.
По состоянию на 20:10 по местному времени специалисты ещё не установили причину возникновения пожара. Взлётно-посадочную полосу после инцидента временно закрыли, однако, по информации японских властей, это не оказало существенного влияния на движение пассажирских рейсов.
По данным сервиса отслеживания полётов Plane Finder, 22 октября в Нагою прибыл Ан-124-100 украинской авиакомпании Antonov Airlines с бортовым номером UR-82029.
Самолет выполнял грузовой рейс ADB5561 из Фербанкса на Аляске в Нагою. Plane Finder идентифицирует его как Antonov An-124-100 и указывает в качестве оператора Antonov Airlines.
В соцсетях пользователи предполагают, что источником пламени мог быть двигатель или вспомогательная силовая установка самолета. Официально причина инцидента остается неизвестной.

title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
content_c:
Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
- Published
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.
The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.
Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.
Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
'Critically important'
Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.
After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.
It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.
And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
content_c:
Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.
Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.
He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.
The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.
Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.
It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.
The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.
The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.
AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.
The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.
The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.
Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”
He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.
The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.
Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.
The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.
According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.
In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.
Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.
In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.
It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.
In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.
At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.

title: Is EU putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?
content_c:
Is EU putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?
October 22, 2026
Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign that relations continue to expand.
The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam's commercial ties with most European states.
Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship "is a welcome advertisement for keeping markets open," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.
"This is a win-win for both sides," he said. "Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs."
Vietnam-EU ties deepen
Vietnam is now the EU's largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam's fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.
Noneconomic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.
Vietnam has become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.
"The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU's economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China," he said, referring to the European Union's efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.
Several EU states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam. Bloc foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.
Concerns over Vietnam's human rights record
The relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam's economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi's worsening human rights record.
Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country's powerful public security ministry.
In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised "grave concerns over the Vietnamese government's intensifying repression" and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.
When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.
These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.
Rights groups say Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.
"The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam's repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations," the joint letter read.
Benefits 'distributed unevenly'
There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU's trade liberalization.
Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe's complex import requirements.
Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.
"It is quite clear that the EVFTA's benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship," Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.
"The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance," he added.
Better for EU?
Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam's expanding export economy.
Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than EU sales to Vietnam.
The EU's goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025 — up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.
This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for EU industries.
Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement, signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.
"We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.
Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.
The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater EU investment in Vietnam.
"With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam's extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish," Humphrey said.
"That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform," he added.
For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that EU businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises.

description: The EU and Vietnam are deepening economic and diplomatic ties, but closer cooperation raises concerns about whether Brussels is doing enough to address Hanoi's human rights record, labor standards and trade imbalances.
content:
Is EU putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?
October 22, 2026
Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign that relations continue to expand.
The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam's commercial ties with most European states.
Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship "is a welcome advertisement for keeping markets open," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.
"This is a win-win for both sides," he said. "Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs."
Vietnam-EU ties deepen
Vietnam is now the EU's largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam's fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.
Noneconomic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.
Vietnam has become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.
"The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU's economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China," he said, referring to the European Union's efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.
Several EU states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam. Bloc foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.
Concerns over Vietnam's human rights record
The relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam's economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi's worsening human rights record.
Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country's powerful public security ministry.
In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised "grave concerns over the Vietnamese government's intensifying repression" and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.
When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.
These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.
Rights groups say Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.
"The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam's repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations," the joint letter read.
Benefits 'distributed unevenly'
There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU's trade liberalization.
Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe's complex import requirements.
Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.
"It is quite clear that the EVFTA's benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship," Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.
"The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance," he added.
Better for EU?
Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam's expanding export economy.
Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than EU sales to Vietnam.
The EU's goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025 — up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.
This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for EU industries.
Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement, signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.
"We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.
Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.
The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater EU investment in Vietnam.
"With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam's extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish," Humphrey said.
"That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform," he added.
For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that EU businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises.

title: Ukraine-Krieg: Trump soll Musk zur Aufhebung der Starlink-Drosselung gedrängt haben
content_c:
Bericht des »Wall Street Journal« Trump soll Musk angewiesen haben, die Starlink-Drosselung aufzuheben
US-Präsident Donald Trump hat einem Medienbericht zufolge SpaceX-Chef Elon Musk gedrängt, die Drosselung des Satelliteninternets Starlink für die Ukraine aufzuheben. Das berichtet das »Wall Street Journal « unter Berufung auf US-Regierungsvertreter. Kurz nach dem Gespräch zwischen Trump und Musk habe das System wieder normaler funktioniert, heißt es weiter.
Auch nach Angaben des US-Präsidenten hat Musk den Zugang zum Satellitennetzwerk inzwischen wieder hergestellt. Als Trump von Reportern gefragt wurde , ob er Musk wegen der Freigabe von Starlink für die Ukraine angerufen habe, wollte er das nicht bestätigen – stritt es jedoch auch nicht ab. »Ob ich oder jemand anderes angerufen hat, macht keinen Unterschied«, so Trump. »Fest steht, er hat es wieder angeschaltet.«
Die Ukraine ist für ihre Kommunikation auf dem Schlachtfeld und den Einsatz von Drohnen auf Starlink angewiesen. Eine Drosselung des Dienstes hatte nach ukrainischen Angaben zuletzt die militärischen Aktivitäten im Kampf gegen Russland eingeschränkt.
Medienberichten zufolge ist Musk für die mutmaßliche Einschränkung der Satellitenkommunikation in der Ukraine verantwortlich. Wie das »Wall Street Journal« (WSJ) und der Sender CBS News unter Berufung auf anonyme US-Regierungsmitarbeiter sowie mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Kreise berichteten , soll Musk eine Einschränkung des Satellitenkommunikationsdiensts für die Ukraine angeordnet haben.
Demnach habe Musk die Geschwindigkeit begrenzt, mit der ukrainische Geräte eine Verbindung zu dem System herstellen könnten. Dies habe dazu geführt, dass schnell fliegende ukrainische Drohnen funktionsunfähig geworden seien, weil sie keine Datenverbindung mehr aufbauen konnten, hieß es in dem »WSJ«-Bericht.
Mehr zum Konflikt zwischen den USA und der Ukraine: Jetzt verzögert Trump auch noch Waffenlieferungen – warum das fatale Folgen für Kyjiw haben könnte .

title: Bevölkerungsschutz: Wie Schweden für den Ernstfall vorsorgt
content_c:
Bevölkerungsschutz Wie Schweden für den Ernstfall vorsorgt
Kriege, Extremwetter, Terror: Schweden bereitet seine Bevölkerung auf den möglichen Ernstfall vor - etwa mit einer Broschüre und Übungen. Denn klar ist auch: Im Fall der Fälle müssen die Menschen erstmal alleine klarkommen.
Ende September im kleinen Örtchen Grums in Mittelschweden: Lars-Göran Wadén erwartet eine spannende Nacht. Zusammen mit rund 40 anderen lässt sich der Rollstuhlfahrer in einem Bunker einschließen.
"Es fühlt sich bedeutsam an, als Person mit einer Behinderung an einer solchen Übung teilzunehmen und seine Erfahrungen teilen zu können", sagt er. Schutzräume lägen normalerweise im Keller, wo es Treppen gebe. "Es geht also darum, wie ich überhaupt dort herunterkomme. Und dann muss man versuchen, irgendwie zur Toilette zu kommen, wenn man länger dort unten ist. Soweit ich weiß, gibt es einfach einen Eimer, auf dem man seine Bedürfnisse in eine Tüte erledigen soll."
Übung im Rahmen der Bereitschaftswoche
Eine Nacht im Bunker ohne fließendes Wasser und Strom, auf Matratzen auf dem Boden - auch für die anderen Teilnehmer keine alltägliche Erfahrung. Die Stimmung ist bei den meisten trotzdem gut. "Ich habe eine richtig gemütliche Ecke gefunden mit viel Platz", sagt etwa Eva Nordström. "Ich habe viele Sachen mitgenommen, eine Stirnlampe zum Beispiel."
Nordström nimmt ebenfalls freiwillig an der Übung im Rahmen der 10. schwedischen Bereitschaftswoche teil. Zu solchen Anlässen engagierten sich viele Kommunen und auch private Unternehmen, unterstreicht Anna Lihr von der schwedischen Behörde für Bevölkerungsschutz:
                
                
                Wir haben in Schweden große Schritte unternommen, um das Bewusstsein dafür zu stärken, wie wichtig Krisenvorsorge ist. Wir heißen heute Behörde für Zivilverteidigung, arbeiten eng mit den Streitkräften zusammen und sprechen wieder viel stärker über die Gesamtverteidigung. So mobilisieren wir die Fähigkeiten der gesamten Gesellschaft.
Konzept aus der Zeit des Kalten Krieges
Gesamtverteidigung heißt: Im Fall eines militärischen Angriffs können alle Menschen in Schweden zwischen 16 und 70 für militärische oder zivile Aufgaben herangezogen werden. Das Konzept stammt noch aus der Zeit des Kalten Krieges.
Was zu tun wäre, wenn das Land angegriffen wird, können die Schweden auch in einer Broschüre nachlesen, die Lihrs Behörde vor einiger Zeit an alle Haushalte verschickt hat. Darin wird zum Beispiel erklärt, wie man sich vor Luftangriffen schützt und welche Vorräte nötig sind, um im Ernstfall sieben Tage ohne Hilfe der Behörden zu überleben. Alarmismus? Nein, sagt Lihr.
                
                
                Es ist natürlich ein Balanceakt. Aber wir müssen darüber sprechen, dass wir es mit einer ernsten Bedrohung zu tun haben. Wir wollen die demokratische Gesellschaft, in der wir leben, schützen. Und wir beobachten in unserer Umgebung eine Entwicklung, die besorgniserregend ist.
Krisenbewusstsein in der Bevölkerung
Sorgen macht den schwedischen Behörden Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine, aber auch hybride Bedrohungen und die zunehmende Gefahr von Extremwetterereignissen. Auch in der Bevölkerung gebe es ein Krisenbewusstsein, sagt Alexander Cedergren, Assistenzprofessor für Gesellschaftssicherheit an der Universität Lund.
                
                
                Viele sind sich der Lage bewusst und sehen, was in der Welt geschieht. Und viele sehen die Notwendigkeit, sich vorzubereiten. Ich glaube, dass die meisten Bürger die Arbeit der Behörden anerkennen. Und gleichzeitig gibt es natürlich Fragen, wie wir uns als Gesellschaft am besten auf verschiedene Arten von Bedrohungen vorbereiten.
Diskutiert wird zum Beispiel, ob neue Schutzräume gebaut werden sollten. 64.000 gibt es schon in Schweden. Sie sollen Platz für etwa 70 Prozent der Bevölkerung bieten. In den vergangenen 20 Jahren seien bei größeren Wohnungsbauprojekten aber keine Schutzräume mehr gebaut worden, sagt Cedergren. Und es seien auch längst nicht alle in Schweden gleich gut auf den Ernstfall vorbereitet.
Krisenübungen wie die in Grums findet der Forscher sinnvoll, darüber sei viel in den Medien berichtet worden. "Das führt zu einer Sensibilisierung und trägt zu einem allgemeinen Krisenbewusstsein bei."
"Ich habe mehr Fragen als vorher"
Nach zwölf Stunden im unterirdischen Bunker sind in Grums alle Teilnehmenden froh, das Tageslicht wiederzusehen. Es sei ein beängstigendes Gefühl, sein Leben in die Hände anderer zu legen, so Rollstuhlfahrer Lars-Göran Wadén: "Ich habe mehr Fragen als vorher. Für Menschen im Rollstuhl ist das hier nicht problemlos zu bewältigen."
Selbst bei vorbildlicher Krisenvorsorge wie in Schweden ist also immer noch Luft nach oben. Eva Nordström jedenfalls ist sich nach der Übung völlig sicher, was sie zuhause als Erstes tun will: "Duschen!"

title: Україну накриває аномальне потепління, але холоднеча вже на порозі: синоптики попередили про зміну погоди в низці міст
content_c:
Україну накриває аномальне потепління, але холоднеча вже на порозі: синоптики попередили про зміну погоди в низці міст
Атмосферний фронт із Західної Європи принесе до України 23 жовтня дощі та тумани.
У п’ятницю, 23 жовтня, в Україні утримуватиметься тепла погода, однак західний атмосферний фронт зумовить підвищену хмарність і дощі в більшості регіонів. Попри періодичні опади й ранкові тумани температурний режим залишатиметься досить комфортним, а на півдні стовпчики термометрів сягатимуть 20 градусів тепла.
Детальний прогноз погоди від синоптиків — читайте в матеріалі ТСН.ua.
Погода в Україні
Керівник Черкаського гідрометцентру Віталій Постригань повідомляє, що в період від 23 до 27 жовтня 2026 року аномальне тепло в регіоні продовжить триматися. Погожий характер істотно не зміниться: переважатиме хмарна погода з періодичними невеликими дощами та ранковими туманами.
Вночі термометри показуватимуть від +6 до +11 градусів тепла, водночас вдень повітря прогріватиметься до комфортних +12…+17 градусів. Згідно з попередніми прогнозами, вже наступного робочого тижня атмосферні потоки почнуть перебудовуватися у бік похолодання, проте різких арктичних вторгнень наразі очікувати не варто.
За даними Українського гідрометцентру, в Україні 23 жовтня на погоду впливатиме атмосферний фронт, який надійшов із Західної Європи.
«Незважаючи на те, що загалом утримуватиметься поле високого тиску (хоча його значення зазнаватимуть деяких коливань у зоні фронту), фронт зумовить вночі на Правобережжі, вдень — у більшості областей, крім заходу і сходу, дощі. Вітер дутиме з південного сходу, лише на заході за фронтом перейде на західний. Переважатиме тепла, як для цієї пори, погода», — повідомляють метеорологи.
Загалом по країні буде хмарно з проясненнями. Вночі на Правобережжі, вдень в Україні, крім заходу та сходу, пройдуть дощі. Вітер дутиме південно-східний, на заході країни — західний зі швидкістю 5–10 м/с.
Температура повітря вночі коливатиметься від +8 до +13 градусів тепла, в західних і східних областях очікується від +4 до +9 градусів. Вдень повітря прогріється до +12…+17 тепла, на півдні країни синоптики прогнозують до +20.
Погода в Києві
У п’ятницю, 23 жовтня, на Київщині буде хмарно з проясненнями, місцями пройдуть дощі. Вітер дутиме південно-східний зі швидкістю 5–10 м/с. Температура повітря по області вночі коливатиметься від +8 до +13 градусів тепла, вдень очікується від +12 до +17 градусів.
У Києві вночі температура повітря становитиме від +11 до +13 градусів тепла, вдень очікується від +14 до +16 градусів вище нуля.
Погода у Львові
На Львівщині 23 жовтня погоду визначатиме проходження атмосферних фронтів із заходу. Буде хмарно з проясненням. Вночі пройде невеликий дощ, вдень істотних опадів не передбачається. description: Атмосферний фронт із Західної Європи принесе до України 23 жовтня дощі та тумани.
content:
Україну накриває аномальне потепління, але холоднеча вже на порозі: синоптики попередили про зміну погоди в низці міст
Атмосферний фронт із Західної Європи принесе до України 23 жовтня дощі та тумани.
У п’ятницю, 23 жовтня, в Україні утримуватиметься тепла погода, однак західний атмосферний фронт зумовить підвищену хмарність і дощі в більшості регіонів. Попри періодичні опади й ранкові тумани температурний режим залишатиметься досить комфортним, а на півдні стовпчики термометрів сягатимуть 20 градусів тепла.

Вночі термометри показуватимуть від +6 до +11 градусів тепла, водночас вдень повітря прогріватиметься до комфортних +12…+17 градусів. Згідно з попередніми прогнозами, вже наступного робочого тижня атмосферні потоки почнуть перебудовуватися у бік похолодання, проте різких арктичних вторгнень наразі очікувати не варто.
За даними Українського гідрометцентру, в Україні 23 жовтня на погоду впливатиме атмосферний фронт, який надійшов із Західної Європи.

title: «Россияне, наверное, умирают со смеху»: ведущий Fox News раскритиковал Уиткоффа за лесть Путину
content_c:
Ведущий Fox News Брайан Килмид опубликовал в социальной сети X видео, в котором раскритиковал заявление специального посланника президента США Стива Уиткоффа, назвавшего российского президента Владимира Путина «гуманистом».
«Россияне, наверное, просто умирали со смеху», — заявил Килмид в видео.
«Такие слова только выставляют вас наивным. Гуманист? Этот человек убивает своих оппонентов, арестовывает журналистов... Дамы и господа, все, кто меня слушает: если вы увидите Владимира Путина, не называйте его гуманистом», — продолжил ведущий.
Путин — бандит, а не гуманист. Смотрите полную версию шоу Брайана Килмида на YouTube https://t.co/gSmsoepLSk @FoxNews @foxnewsradio https://t.co/m6iFeBFtJ8
— Брайан Килмид (@kilmeade) 22 октября 2026
Килмид отреагировал на слова Уиткоффа, обращённые к Путину в российском Санкт-Петербурге после освобождения в среду американца Стивена Габбарда.
«Вы так много говорите о моём президенте, президенте Трампе, называя его гуманистом, — сказал Уиткофф Путину. — Вы тоже гуманист, господин, и я выражаю вам своё уважение».
Габбарда освободили в среду, и он уже вернулся в Соединенные Штаты после почти четырёх лет заключения в России.
Рано утром в четверг он прибыл на авиабазу Лекленд в Сан-Антонио.
Президент Дональд Трамп заявил, что лично попросил российского диктатора освободить Габбарда во время телефонного разговора, а Уиткофф отправился в Россию, чтобы добиться его освобождения.
Заявление Уиткоффа вызвало волну критики со стороны различных политических лагерей, в том числе и со стороны республиканцев.

title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
content_c:
'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
- Published
Clavicular, a social media influencer who promotes the "looksmaxxing" trend of young men maximising their attractiveness, has pleaded not guilty to criminal charges including rape.
The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Peters, was charged in September with felony rape, drugging an individual for sexual intercourse and procuring alcohol for someone under the age of 21.
The charges stem from an incident in 2025 when he is accused of assaulting a 17-year-old girl at his family's Massachusetts home.
Peters has denied the allegations and said the encounter was consensual. On Thursday, he was granted $10,000 bail, ordered not to contact or post about his accuser, and to surrender his passport.
A woman told police that on 23 May 2025, Peters ordered her an Uber to his family's house in Chatham where they were drinking alcohol while filming a livestream before he allegedly raped her, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
The police officer who took the report said he believed she was unable to consent due to her age and the level of intoxication she exhibited in the livestream, CBS reported.
Clavicular has more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and has garnered media attention for extreme measures he has taken for "looksmaxxing".
He has admitted to using a hammer on his face and jawline and taking a number of steroids, injections, and other drugs to achieve bodily perfection. He also gives advice on appearing masculine and performs stunts to shock followers.
In Florida earlier this year, he was charged after filming himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator. He pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public.
In March, he was arrested on suspicion of battery after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities said in July that they did not intend to file charges.
After Thursday's hearing, Peters posted a photo of himself in the black suit and black tie he wore to court, while holding his dog which he also brought to court.
His next hearing will be on 24 November, when the judge will decide if there is enough evidence for the case to move forward.

title: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
content_c:
The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield.
Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”
The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.
Media outlets – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.
However, in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and said the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.
Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport which was the kingdom’s deadliest in years as the war with the group escalates.
On Thursday the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that two people had been killed in overnight attacks on King Fahd international airport in Dammam on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
Eight people were injured and there was material damage to the airport, according to officials. The global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.
Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The Houthis said on Thursday they had launched attacks on Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry in Riyadh, Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and King Fahd international airport in Dammam.
Essential workers at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in the east of the country were told to evacuate on Thursday, two sources told Agence France-Presse, after their non-essential colleagues were told to work from home since last week.
The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf in late February before the start of its war against Iran. NBC reported that the US military had been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, but a spokesperson from US central command told the US news outlet that service members were regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
The withdrawal of staff from the region coincides with reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
The New York Times reported that the US and Israel had developed plans for a “short but intensive operation” after the defense secretary, Peter Hegseth, travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Last week Trump said the US was hoping to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a site linked to the country’s nuclear program, however the US president has publicly said he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse
